p: **Kuzey Aydın,** 11. Lives in Kadıköy, Istanbul, with his grandmother while his parents study penguins in Antarctica. Has heard the wind whispering his whole life. Thinks he is completely normal. He is wrong.
**Ela Aydın,** 12. Kuzey's cousin. Braids, glasses, a pencil behind each ear. Keeps the Clue Book and writes down *everything.* Wants to be a detective, a spy and a codebreaker, possibly all at once.
**Bora Kaya,** 11. Kuzey's best friend since the first day of first grade. The biggest kid in the class and the kindest. Always hungry. Has a cousin in every city in the world.
**Grandma Nermin.** Kuzey's grandmother. Small, silver-haired, very sharp. Makes the best börek in Kadıköy. Never takes off her bronze necklace. Has some secrets.
**Uncle Tarık.** Ela's father. An archaeologist with wild hair, a dusty jacket and a lot of airline miles.
**Mordecai Vane.** A tall man in a long gray coat, with a gray glove on his right hand. You do not want to see what is under the glove.
**Vex and Vera Vane,** 13. Twins. Pale hair, cold green eyes. Vex likes to win. Vera likes to ask questions.

chapters.t: Chapter One: The Wind Knows My Name
p: Most kids in Istanbul hear the wind as noise. It rattles windows, steals hats on the ferry and slams doors so hard your mom thinks you did it on purpose.
I hear words.

Not all the time. Only on days when the wind blows hard off the Bosphorus and the seagulls give up flying and just sit on the lamp posts looking annoyed. On those days, if I close my eyes, the wind whispers. Mostly it says boring things, like *rain soon* or *the bakery on the corner is burning the simit again*. Once it told me where my lost football was. (Under the neighbor's car. The wind was right.)

My name is Kuzey Aydın. I am eleven years old, and *Kuzey* means North. My grandmother picked that name. She said it was because I was born on the coldest night of the year, while the north wind howled over the city like a happy wolf.
I believed her. Until the day of the Poyraz storm, when everything I believed got blown away.
But before I tell you about that day, you need to know three things about me, or nothing else will make sense.

The first thing is that I live with my grandmother. My mom and dad are marine biologists, which means they study things that live in the sea. Right now they are on a research ship near Antarctica, counting penguins and measuring ice, and they will not be home for a whole year. They call me every Sunday on a video call that freezes every ten seconds, so mostly I talk to a frozen picture of my dad with his mouth open. It's fine. I'm used to it. Mostly.

The second thing is that I have never told anyone about the wind. Not my parents. Not my teachers. Not even my best friend. When I was six, I told a boy in my class that the wind had told me it was going to rain at lunchtime, and he laughed so hard that milk came out of his nose, and then it rained at lunchtime, and he never spoke to me again. After that, I kept the wind to myself.
The third thing is that the wind had been acting strange for a whole week before the storm. Louder. More nervous. Like a dog that hears thunder before you do.
On Monday, it whispered *something is coming* while I was walking to school.

On Tuesday, it blew my homework out of my hands, all the way across the schoolyard, and dropped it at the feet of the only person in the world who could get me in more trouble than my homework: my cousin Ela.
On Wednesday, it said *watch the gray ones* and nothing else, over and over, until I put my hands over my ears in the middle of math class and Ms. Demir asked if I had a headache.
On Thursday, I saw my first gray one.

He was standing on the corner across from my school, next to the man who sells roasted chestnuts. A tall man in a gray suit, with a gray hat, holding a gray umbrella even though it wasn't raining. He wasn't buying chestnuts. He wasn't waiting for the bus. He was just standing there, looking at the school gate.
Looking at *me.*
When I looked back, he didn't look away. His eyes were a strange color, pale and cloudy, like fog on a window. Then a bus went past between us, and when it had gone, so had he.
The chestnut man was coughing. His little cart was covered in frost. In Istanbul. In November. When it was fifteen degrees outside.
*The gray ones,* whispered the wind, very softly. *They are looking for you, little one. Be careful.*
I didn't tell anyone about that either.
Maybe I should have.

It was a Saturday in November. I was at Grandma Nermin's apartment in Kadıköy with my cousin Ela and my best friend Bora. Grandma's apartment is on the fifth floor of an old building with a wooden door, a creaky elevator that nobody trusts, and a cat called Paşa who lives on the stairs and belongs to nobody.

It's also where I live now, since my parents left for the ice. I like it. The apartment is full of old maps, brass instruments, glass jars of strange seeds, books in languages I can't read, and a tea kettle that has been boiling since before I was born. Grandma says a kitchen without boiling tea is just a room with a fridge in it.
"Kuzey," said Ela, without looking up from her notebook. "Your grandmother has nine compasses on that shelf. Nine. Who needs nine compasses?"

Ela is twelve. She is my cousin, the daughter of my Uncle Tarık. She has two long braids, glasses she pushes up with one finger like a detective, and a notebook she calls the Clue Book. She writes down everything. *Everything.* Once she wrote down what Bora ate in a single day. It took two pages.

She wants to be a detective when she grows up. Or a spy. Or a codebreaker. Or possibly all three at the same time. She has read every mystery book in the Kadıköy library, some of them twice, and she can solve a Sudoku faster than my calculator.
"Maybe she gets lost a lot," said Bora, who was eating his fourth börek.

Bora Kaya is the biggest kid in our class and the kindest. He is also always hungry. Scientists should study him. He has been my best friend since the first day of first grade, when a bigger kid pushed me off the swing and Bora, who was already bigger than the bigger kid, walked over and sat on the swing next to me and said, "Do you want half my sandwich?" Then he gave me the whole sandwich. That's Bora.
He is also afraid of exactly three things: the dark, heights and running out of food. Remember that. It becomes important later.
"Grandma never gets lost," I said. "She once found her way home from Kapalıçarşı in a blackout. Without a phone."
"That's impossible," said Ela. "The Grand Bazaar has four thousand shops and sixty-one streets. People get lost in there *with* phones."
"She said the wind showed her the way."
Ela wrote that down. Then she looked at it for a long moment and crossed it out.

Grandma was in the kitchen making more börek, singing an old song from the Black Sea in her crackly voice. Through the window, I could see the Bosphorus, the long blue river of sea that cuts Istanbul in half, with Europe on one side and Asia on the other. Ferries crossed it like white beetles. Seagulls floated over it. On the far side, the old city sat on its hills, covered in domes and minarets.
It was a normal Saturday. The most normal Saturday in the history of Saturdays.
That was when the windows started to rattle.

Outside, the sky over the Bosphorus turned the color of a bruise. It happened fast. One minute there was sun on the water, and the next, a wall of purple-black cloud came rolling down from the north, from the Black Sea, swallowing the bridges one by one.
"Poyraz," said Bora, looking out the window. "My dad says when the Poyraz comes, the fishermen go home."
The wind came screaming down the Bosphorus. The ferries rocked. A man on the street below lost his umbrella, and it flew past our fifth-floor window, upside down, like a bat.
And every one of Grandma's nine compasses began to spin.
Not just wobble. *Spin.* Round and round, faster and faster, their needles blurring like tiny propellers, buzzing like angry bees.
"Kuzey," said Ela slowly. "Compasses don't do that."
And under the howl, I heard it. Not a whisper this time. Clear as a voice on the phone.
*Kuzey. Wake up, Windborn. They are coming for the Keeper.*
I dropped my tea glass.
It didn't break. It floated.
For one second, the glass hung in the air on a little spinning cushion of wind, right in front of my nose, with the tea still inside it, turning slowly like a tiny planet.
Then it fell and smashed, and Bora said a word his mother would not have liked.

Ela had stopped writing. She was staring at me, and for once in her life, she didn't have anything clever to say. Her mouth opened and closed a few times. Then she said, very quietly, "Kuzey. Did you just do that?"
"I don't know," I said. And that was the truth.
Before I could say anything else, Grandma Nermin came out of the kitchen.

She is small, with silver hair tied in a bun and very sharp brown eyes, and she wears a necklace with a bronze compass needle on it that she never takes off. Not in the shower. Not when she sleeps. I asked her about it once, and she said, "It's a very old present from a very old friend," and changed the subject to my homework.
She looked at the spinning compasses. She looked at the broken glass. She looked at me.
And she didn't look surprised at all.
She looked *scared.*

I had never seen my grandmother scared. Not when the earthquake shook the building when I was eight. Not when I fell off my bike and needed six stitches. Not when the man at the fish market tried to sell her a three-day-old bluefish. My grandmother is not scared of anything.
"So," she said quietly. "It has started. I hoped we had more time."

chapters.t: Chapter Three: The Order of the Compass Rose
p: Grandma closed the curtains. She locked the front door, then locked it again with a big old key that I had never seen her use. Then she did something that had never happened in recorded history.
She turned off the kettle.
Bora gasped. Ela dropped her pencil. Even Paşa the cat, who had come in through the window to escape the storm, stopped licking his paw and stared.
"Sit down," said Grandma. "All of you. Listen carefully. Because I may only have time to say this once."
We sat down at the kitchen table. Outside, the storm howled. The nine compasses had stopped spinning, but now all nine needles were pointing in the same direction: not north, but straight at me.
Grandma took off her necklace and laid the bronze needle on the table.

I had seen it a thousand times, but never this close. It was about as long as my hand, covered in tiny engraved letters in an alphabet I didn't know, and one end was shaped like a star. When I reached out to touch it, I gasped. It was cold. Not cold like metal from the fridge. Cold like the inside of a cloud, like the top of a mountain, like the air on the coldest night of the year.

"Thousands of years ago," Grandma said, "the seven great winds of the world were wild. Nobody could predict them. Nobody could control them. They wrecked ships, flattened cities, made deserts out of forests and forests out of swamps. People lived in fear of the sky."
The storm rattled the windows, as if it was listening.

"So the wise people of many lands came together. Persians and Greeks, Egyptians and Chinese, Turks and Vikings and many more, whose names are forgotten. They forged seven bronze Keys, and with them they made a deal with the winds. The strongest part of each wind, its heart, would sleep inside one Key. In return, the people promised never to use the winds for war or greed. Then they hid the Keys across the whole world, and in a secret place they built a Gate. The Gate of Seven Winds. It can only open when all seven Keys are together."
"What happens if it opens?" asked Bora, with his mouth full. Even in a crisis, Bora eats.

"Whoever holds the Gate open controls the weather of the whole world. Every storm. Every drought. Every flood. Every gentle rain that makes the wheat grow." Grandma tapped the needle. "Imagine one person deciding which countries get rain and which countries get nothing. Who gets hurricanes. Who gets sunshine. That person would be the most powerful person who ever lived. And the most dangerous."
Nobody said anything for a while.

"Our family belongs to a secret society called the Order of the Compass Rose," Grandma went on. "For nine hundred years, we have kept the Keys hidden. Each Key has a Keeper, and the Keepers pass them down, mother to daughter, father to son, teacher to student. I am the Keeper of this one: the Yıldız Key. The key of the North Wind."
"Yıldız," said Ela slowly. "That means *star.*"
"The north wind is named after the North Star," said Grandma. "Because it blows from under it."

Ela was writing so fast her pencil smoked. "Seven winds," she muttered. "Like the old Turkish wind rose. Sailors used it for hundreds of years. Yıldız from the north. Poyraz from the northeast. Gündoğusu from the east, where the sun rises. Keşişleme from the southeast. Kıble from the south. Lodos from the southwest. Karayel from the northwest." She looked up. "That's seven. But a normal compass has eight directions. The west is missing."

"Clever girl," said Grandma, and she actually smiled. "Yes. Each Key is named for one of them. And the west wind is missing because the west wind was the one that would not make a deal. It is still wild, even now. That's another story, for another day."
"And Kuzey?" I said. My voice came out squeaky. "I mean, me. The wind called me something. It called me a Windborn. What's a Windborn?"
Grandma reached across the table and held my hands. Hers were trembling.

"Once in a hundred years," she said, "a child of the Order is born who can hear the winds. Who can talk to them. And one day, if he is brave and kind and patient, command them. A Windborn. You are the first one since your great-great-grandfather, Kaptan Murat Aydın, who sailed the Black Sea in a boat with no engine and never once lost his way."
"You knew?" I said. "This whole time, you *knew?*"

"I hoped," she said. "Ever since the night you were born, when the north wind came through the window of the hospital and sang. The nurses said it was the heating. I knew better." She squeezed my hands. "I wanted to tell you when you were older. Thirteen, maybe. I wanted you to have a few more years of being just a boy."
"Why?"
"Because the winds will help you find the hidden Keys," she said. "And that is exactly why someone else wants you."
"Who?"
The doorbell rang.
It was not a normal ring.

It went on and on, a long electric scream that didn't stop, like someone was leaning on the button with their whole body. The lights in the kitchen flickered. The ceiling lamp swung on its chain. Paşa the cat hissed and shot under the sofa.
And the temperature dropped.
I could see my breath. Frost crawled across the inside of the kitchen window, white and feathery, spreading like a living thing. The tea in the pot on the table grew a thin skin of ice.
Grandma's face went pale.
"Mordecai Vane," she whispered.
"Who's that?" said Bora.

"The leader of the Ashen Circle. A group of people who believe the winds should be owned, not protected. He has wanted the Keys for forty years." She stood up. Her eyes were very bright. "And I am the only Keeper in this city."
The doorbell stopped. In the silence, I heard footsteps on the stairs. Many footsteps. Slow, heavy, all in step, like soldiers.
Grandma moved fast for an old lady. She picked up the bronze needle and pressed the Yıldız Key into my hand. It was so cold it burned. She closed my fingers around it with both of her hands.

"Kuzey, listen to me. This Key is only the first. There are six more, and he wants them all. You must find them before he does. Your first clue is in the place where Medusa stands on her head. Do you understand?"
"No!"
"You will. You are cleverer than you think. And Ela is cleverer than both of us." She kissed my forehead. "Ela, Bora, stay with him. Whatever happens, stay with him."
§CLUE Your first clue is in the place where Medusa stands on her head. (Grandma Nermin, in the kitchen, just before the door froze.)
"Grandma, come with us!"

"I can't. If I run, he will follow. If I stay, I can slow him down." She went to the kitchen window and pushed it open. The storm blew in, wild and wet, scattering papers everywhere. Outside was the old iron fire escape that zigzagged down the back of the building. "Go out the window. Down the fire stairs. Do *not* come back for me. No matter what you hear."
The footsteps stopped outside the front door.
Somebody knocked. Three slow knocks.
"Nermin," said a voice through the door. A man's voice, smooth and polite, like someone selling expensive carpets. "It's been a long time. May I come in?"
"No," said Grandma.
"I thought you might say that."
The front door exploded inward.

Not like in movies, with fire and smoke. It froze. In a single second, the whole wooden door turned white with frost, and then it shattered into a thousand pieces of ice that skittered across the hallway floor like broken glass.
A man walked in as if he owned the place.

He was tall and thin, in a long gray coat that reached almost to his ankles. His hair was dark, with gray streaks at the sides. His face was handsome, I suppose, the way a statue is handsome: smooth and cold and perfectly still. And his right hand wore a gray leather glove that seemed to drink the light around it.

Behind him came two kids about thirteen years old, a boy and a girl. They had the same pale blond hair, the same sharp faces, the same cold green eyes. Twins. The boy was grinning like this was the best day of his life. The girl was not grinning at all.

And behind the twins, filling the stairway, were the gray men. Six of them, maybe more, in identical gray suits and gray hats. Their eyes were pale and cloudy, exactly like the man I had seen outside my school.
The gray ones.
"Nermin," said the man, smiling. His smile was the worst thing I had ever seen. It had too many teeth in it. "Forty years, and you still make tea for burglars."
"Mordecai," said Grandma. She stood in the kitchen doorway, blocking it with her tiny body. She came up to about his chest. "You are not welcome in my house."
"I rarely am, anywhere." He took off his glove, one finger at a time.
His hand underneath was gray. Not pale. *Gray,* like stone, like a statue's hand, with little cracks running across the knuckles. Cold mist curled off his fingers and drifted to the floor.
"Vex. Vera," he said, without looking at the twins. "Find the boy."
We were already out the window.

Bora went first, because he said if the fire stairs could hold him, they could hold anyone. They creaked a lot. They groaned. One of the bolts holding them to the wall shot out and pinged off a satellite dish. But they held.
Bora, remember, is afraid of heights. He went down those stairs with his eyes shut, holding the rail with both hands, saying "I'm fine, I'm fine, I'm fine" on every step.
Ela went second, with the Clue Book in her teeth.
I went last.

The storm hit me like a wall the moment I climbed out. Rain smashed into my face. The wind screamed in my ears, and inside the scream I could hear words, hundreds of words, all of them saying the same thing: *Run, Windborn. Run, run, run.*
I looked back once.
Through the kitchen window, I saw Mordecai raise his gray hand. A freezing fog poured out of his fingers and filled the kitchen, swallowing the table, the chairs, the boiling kettle.

And then my grandmother, my tiny, silver-haired grandmother who makes börek and sings Black Sea songs and gets cross when I don't wear a scarf, shouted a word I didn't know. An old word. A word that sounded like wind in a ship's sails.
Every one of her nine compasses flew off the shelf and hit Mordecai in the face.
*Bonk. Bonk. Bonk. Bonk.*

He staggered backwards, his arms up. A brass compass bounced off his nose. Another one hit one of the gray men in the stomach, and he folded over like a deckchair. It would have been funny if I wasn't so terrified.
"Go, Kuzey!" Grandma shouted, without turning around. "GO!"
Then the fog swallowed everything.
I heard a crash. A cry. A long, cold silence.

When the fog cleared, the kitchen was empty. Grandma was gone. Mordecai stood alone in the middle of the frosted kitchen, holding her necklace chain in his gray hand, the empty chain swinging back and forth. He looked up at the window. At me.
And he laughed.
"Run, little Windborn!" he called out of the window, as if we were playing a game. "Run and find the Keys for me! It will save me so much work!"
Something in my chest broke. I wanted to climb back in. I wanted to scream at him, hit him, make the storm smash him through the wall. I actually started back up the stairs.
Ela grabbed my ankle from below. Hard.
"Kuzey," she said, through the Clue Book in her teeth. "She told you to run. *Run.*"
So I ran.

We ran down five floors of rusty iron stairs, the whole thing shaking and swaying in the wind. We jumped the last two meters into a courtyard full of very surprised cats. We ran through a gate, down an alley full of rubbish bins, and out into the crowded streets of Kadıköy, where the Poyraz storm was blowing so hard that umbrellas turned inside out like flowers and the fruit sellers were chasing oranges down the hill.
Behind us, I heard footsteps. Fast ones. Light ones.
The twins.
"Left!" Ela shouted. "Ferry station!"

The ferry station was at the bottom of the hill, by the water. A ferry was waiting there, its engine rumbling, its horn giving a long, low hoot. *Last call.* We pushed through the crowd, through the ticket gates (Bora jumped his, because he couldn't find his travel card, and a man shouted at him), and ran down the long ramp.
The ramp was already lifting.
"JUMP!" I yelled.
We jumped. Ela made it easily. I made it with a stumble. Bora made it by about one centimeter, landing on the deck with a crash that made the whole ferry rock and three old ladies scream.
Behind us, the twins skidded to a stop at the edge of the dock.

The boy, Vex, shook his fist at us. He was shouting something, but the wind tore his words away. The girl, Vera, just stood still and watched me with her strange green eyes. She didn't look angry like her brother. She looked curious.
And maybe, I thought, a little sad.
The ferry pulled away into the storm.

chapters.t: Chapter Six: The Ferry in the Storm
p: Nobody spoke for a long time.

We sat on the plastic seats at the back of the ferry, inside where it was warm, dripping onto the floor. The ferry rolled and pitched in the big gray waves. Out the windows, the Asian side of Istanbul slowly got smaller, and somewhere in it, on the fifth floor of an old building, was an empty kitchen full of frost.

A tea seller came around with his little tray of tulip-shaped glasses, like he does on every ferry, storm or no storm. Bora bought three teas without asking us, and gave us one each. I held mine in both hands and didn't drink it. My hands were shaking too much.
Then I opened my other hand.
The Yıldız Key lay in my palm. It was humming softly, like a fridge in the night. Frost had formed around it on my skin in the shape of a star.

"Okay," said Bora finally, breathing hard. "Okay. Let me get this straight. Your grandma is a secret agent. A creepy guy with a stone hand kidnapped her. His kids chased us. There were men with fog eyes. And we have a magic needle that makes your hand cold." He took a big gulp of tea. "Did I miss anything?"
"The part where Kuzey can control the wind," said Ela.
"Right," said Bora. "Yes. That part."
They both looked at me.

So I told them. Everything. The whispers I had heard my whole life. The football under the car. The boy with milk coming out of his nose. The gray man outside the school, and the frost on the chestnut cart. I talked and talked, and it was like something heavy that I had been carrying for years was finally being put down.
When I finished, Ela was writing in the Clue Book. Bora was staring at me.
"Why didn't you ever tell me?" he said. He didn't sound angry. He sounded hurt, which was worse.
"I thought you'd think I was crazy."
Bora thought about this. "I do think you're crazy," he said. "But I already thought that before. You put ketchup on börek." He held out his fist. "Still best friends?"
I bumped it with mine. "Still best friends."

"I believe you too," said Ela, without looking up. "Obviously. I saw the glass float. I'm a scientist. Scientists believe evidence." She tapped her pencil on the page. "The question isn't whether it's true. The question is what we do now."
"We have to go to the police," said Bora.

"And tell them what?" said Ela. "'Hello, officer, a man with a stone hand froze a door and kidnapped Kuzey's grandmother with magic fog'? They'll call our parents and send us home. And then Mordecai will find Kuzey, and take the Key, and that'll be the end."
I looked at the Key in my hand. I thought of Grandma's face. *You must find them before he does.*
"Medusa," I said. "She said our first clue is where Medusa stands on her head."
Ela frowned. "Medusa is from Greek mythology. A monster with snakes for hair. Anyone who looks at her turns to stone. But why would she be standing on her head? Is it a riddle? Some kind of code?"
But I already knew. Every kid in Istanbul does. We've all been there on school trips, and every single kid has stood in front of that strange upside-down face in the dark and gotten goosebumps.
"It's not a riddle," I said. "It's a place."
Ela stared at me. Then her eyes went wide behind her glasses, and she slapped her own forehead. "Of course. Of *course!* How did I not see it?"
"See what?" said Bora. "I don't see anything. I see tea."
"The Basilica Cistern," said Ela and I at the same time.

The ferry's horn blew, long and low. Through the rain-streaked windows, the old city was rising out of the storm in front of us: the great domes of Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque, the towers of Topkapı Palace, the minarets like needles stitching the clouds to the hills.
And somewhere under all of that, in the dark, in the water, Medusa was waiting.
As the ferry bumped against the dock at Eminönü, the wind came in through a broken window and brushed my cheek, light as a feather.
*Well done, Windborn,* it whispered. *But be quick. The gray ones know the city too.*

chapters.t: Chapter Seven: Where Medusa Stands on Her Head
p: The Basilica Cistern is a giant underground water palace from the time of the Byzantine Empire, fifteen hundred years old. The emperors built it to store water for the whole city, in case of war or drought. It has three hundred and thirty-six stone columns standing in dark water, lit by orange lights, with fat goldfish swimming between them. It is the spookiest, most beautiful place in Istanbul.

And at the very back, two columns stand on giant stone heads of Medusa. Nobody knows exactly why. Some people say the builders just needed stones of the right size, so they took old statues from ruined temples. Some people say the heads were put there to protect the water from evil.
One head is lying on its side.
The other is upside down.
Standing on her head.

It was almost closing time when we got there, soaking wet, our shoes squelching. The storm had chased all the tourists away. The man at the ticket desk was asleep with his head on his arms, snoring, and the door was open, so we just walked in.
"This is technically not breaking in," whispered Ela, "because the door was open and nobody told us not to."
Ela has a lawyer brain.

We went down the long stone staircase into the dark. The air changed. It was cool and wet and smelled of old stone and older water. The sound of the storm faded behind us until there was only the drip, drip, drip of water from the ceiling and the soft echo of our footsteps on the wooden walkway.

The columns went on forever in every direction, like a forest made of stone. The orange lights at their feet turned the water to gold and threw tall wobbly shadows on the arched ceiling. Fat goldfish, some of them as long as my arm, drifted slowly through the water and watched us with round eyes.
"I don't like this," Bora whispered. "I don't like the dark, and I don't like this. Medusa turns people into stone. I don't want to be a statue. Statues can't eat."
"She's just a carving, Bora," said Ela. "She can't hurt you."
"That's what people always say in movies. Right before they get eaten."

We walked deeper and deeper into the stone forest. The walkway twisted between the columns. Every few meters, there was a little sign in five languages telling us not to throw coins in the water. There were thousands of coins in the water anyway, glittering on the bottom like treasure.
Then the walkway turned one last corner, and there she was.
The upside-down Medusa.

Close up, she was huge, bigger than a car. Her face was carved from pale stone, her hair a mass of twisting stone snakes. Her eyes were wide and blank and staring. Upside down, her face looked even stranger, as if she was hanging from the ceiling, watching us with those empty eyes. The column rose from the top of her head, which was at the bottom, into the dark.
Water lapped softly against her chin, which was at the top.
Nobody spoke.
I knelt down on the walkway. My heart was hammering so hard I could hear it.
And as soon as I knelt, the wind came.

Not outside wind. There was no outside here. This was wind *inside* the cistern, coming from nowhere, cool and gentle, moving across the water in a little ripple. The orange lights flickered. The goldfish scattered.
*Windborn,* it whispered. It was an old voice. Older than any wind I had ever heard, as old as the stones, tired and slow. *I have waited a long time. Put the North into her eye.*
"It's talking again," I told the others. My voice came out as a whisper. "It says to put the North into her eye."
"The North," said Ela slowly. "The North Wind. The Yıldız Key."

She pointed with her flashlight. The beam shook a little. In the center of Medusa's left eye, worn almost smooth by centuries of water, was a small slot. A thin, straight slot, with a little star shape at one end.
Exactly the shape of the Key.

chapters.t: Chapter Eight: The Eye of Medusa
p: I lay on my stomach on the wet wooden walkway, reached down over the black water, and held the Yıldız Key above Medusa's stone eye.
My hand was shaking. The Key was so cold that my fingers had gone numb. Below me, the water was dark and still, and I couldn't see the bottom. I tried not to think about what might be down there.
"Careful," whispered Ela.
"Don't drop it," whispered Bora.
"I'm not going to drop it," I whispered back, and I nearly dropped it.
I slid the Yıldız Key into Medusa's eye.
*Click.*
For a moment, nothing happened. The drip of water. The soft hum of the lights. Bora breathing very loudly through his nose.
Then the stone head groaned.

It was a deep, grinding sound, like a giant clearing its throat. The water around Medusa began to swirl, slowly at first, then faster, until it was spinning around her head like a little whirlpool. Coins rattled across the bottom. Goldfish fled in every direction.
And slowly, with a sound like a heavy door that hasn't been opened in a thousand years, a stone panel slid open on the cheek of the head.
Inside was a little bronze box, green with age, about the size of a pencil case.

I pulled the Key back out of Medusa's eye first. It came out easily, warmer now, almost friendly. Then I reached into the hole in her cheek and lifted out the box. It was heavy. Water dripped from it.
We sat down on the walkway in a tight circle, the box between us. Ela opened it with shaking fingers. The hinges squeaked.
Inside lay two things.
A rolled-up piece of parchment, tied with a faded blue ribbon.
And a second bronze needle, smaller than the Yıldız Key, broken in half. Only the top half was there, with a jagged edge where it had snapped.
"A broken Key?" said Bora. "That's a bit disappointing. Did someone sit on it?"
"No," said Ela. She had untied the ribbon and was reading the parchment, holding it close to her flashlight. "It's not a Key. It's a pointer. Like a key to a key. Listen."
She read it aloud:
§CLUE Seven winds, seven Keys, one Gate. To find the North, climb where Galata's guards once watched for fire, and look where the sun dies at the hour of the evening prayer.
"Galata," I said. "Galata Tower."

"Watched for fire," Ela murmured. "Climb. Sun dies. Evening prayer." She was already copying it into the Clue Book, word for word. Her handwriting is very small and very neat. (She says it's always neat. Bora says it looks like ants walking through ink. They have argued about this for years.)
"But wait," said Bora. "It says 'to find the North.' We already found the North. Kuzey's holding it."
Ela stopped writing.
"He's right," she said slowly. "Why would the clue tell us to find the North if we already have the North Key?"
"Maybe it's not that kind of north," I said. I was thinking of what Grandma had said. *This Key is only the first.* "Maybe it means... where to go next? Like, which direction?"
"Or maybe it's a test," said Ela. "Maybe the Order hid the clues so only the right person could follow them. Someone who could open the box in the first place." She looked at me. "A Windborn."
I looked down at the Yıldız Key in my hand. It was humming again, softly, like it agreed.
And then, from the far end of the cistern, something very large stood up out of the water.

I have read the old Turkish stories of Dede Korkut. Everyone has, in school. We had to learn them in fourth grade, and there was a test, and I got a seventy-eight, which Grandma said was "fine, but your great-great-grandfather would have gotten a hundred."

My favorite story was always the one about Tepegöz. He was a giant with a single eye in the middle of his forehead, who lived in a cave and ate whole flocks of sheep, and then whole villages, and could not be hurt by any sword or arrow. Every warrior who fought him lost. Until a hero called Basat came, and found the giant's one weak spot.
I always liked that story because Basat wasn't the biggest or the strongest. He was just the cleverest.
But I never thought it was *real.*

He rose out of the dark water between the columns, slowly, the water pouring off his shoulders like waterfalls. He was three times taller than a man. His head almost touched the arched ceiling. His skin was gray and wet like a river stone, covered in green slime and little shells. Water weeds hung from his arms. He wore what looked like an old sail tied around his waist, black with age.
And in the middle of his forehead, his one enormous eye glowed a sick yellow, like a streetlight in fog.
It was looking straight at us.

"Little thieves," he rumbled. His voice was so deep that the water shivered and the coins on the bottom rattled. "I have slept beneath this city for a thousand years. The Gray Hand woke me. He promised me sheep. Many, many sheep." He licked his lips with a gray tongue as big as a carpet. "Give me the needles, and I will only eat one of you."
"That's a terrible deal," said Bora.
"Which one?" said Ela. I think she was in shock. She was holding her pencil like she was going to write the answer down.

The giant took a step toward us through the water. His foot hit the base of a column, and the column cracked straight up the middle with a sound like a gunshot. Stones fell from the ceiling and crashed into the water with enormous splashes. Waves rolled across the cistern and slapped against the walkway. The goldfish fled.
"Run!" Ela shouted.
We ran.

The wooden walkway was slippery and narrow, and it twisted between the columns like a maze. We ran back the way we came, our feet pounding, our flashlights swinging wildly, throwing crazy shadows everywhere. Behind us, Tepegöz waded through the water, smashing columns aside with his arms like they were made of breadsticks.
He was faster than us. Much faster. One step of his was ten of ours.
A shadow fell over us. A hand the size of a bathtub came down from above.
Bora was at the back, because Bora is big and big people don't run fast. The giant's fingers closed around Bora's backpack and lifted him straight up into the air, his legs kicking.
"KUZEY!" Bora screamed. "HE'S GOT ME! HE'S GOT ME AND I'M HIGH UP!"
Two of his three fears at once. The dark *and* heights.
Tepegöz lifted Bora up toward his face. Toward his mouth.
"Mmm," rumbled the giant. "A big one. Good. Big ones are the juiciest."
"Put him DOWN!" I yelled.

I didn't think. There was no time to think. I just threw out my hand toward the giant, the hand holding the Yıldız Key, and I *wanted* the wind to help me. Wanted it more than I had ever wanted anything. More than I wanted my parents to come home. More than I wanted Grandma back.
And it did.
A gust of wind exploded out of my palm.
It was so strong that it knocked me flat on my back on the walkway. It roared across the water, white with frost, spraying ice crystals everywhere, and hit Tepegöz right in his giant yellow eye.

The monster roared. It was the loudest sound I have ever heard, louder than a plane taking off, and it echoed around the cistern until the whole place seemed to be roaring. He dropped Bora, who fell about four meters and landed in the water with a splash like a whale, and clutched his face with both hands.
"His eye!" Ela shouted. "In the story, Basat beats Tepegöz by blinding his eye! It's his only weak spot!"
I got up. My hand was tingling and freezing, and there was a thin layer of frost on my sleeve all the way to my elbow. The Key was glowing in my fingers like a tiny blue star.

The giant was blinking, his eye streaming huge tears, swinging his fists wildly. One fist smashed the walkway right where Ela had been standing a second before. Wood exploded. Ela leaped to the next section of walkway and grabbed a railing.
"Bora!" I shouted. "Where are you?"
"Here!" Bora's head popped up out of the water next to a column. He was spitting out water and a goldfish. "Kuzey! The lights! Do the wind thing at the lights!"
I looked down. At the bottom of every column, there was a big, bright orange spotlight, pointing up to light the stone. Three hundred and thirty-six columns. Hundreds of lights.
Bora was right. Bora, soaking wet, in the water with a giant, terrified of the dark, was thinking more clearly than either of us.
I closed my eyes.
I listened.
And under the roaring of the giant and the crashing of the water, I heard it. The wind inside the cistern. Old and slow and tired, swirling between the columns, waiting.
*Help me,* I asked it. *Please.*
*Gladly, Windborn,* it whispered back. *I have been bored for a thousand years.*
I swept my arm in a wide circle.

And the wind went everywhere at once. It rushed through the cistern like a wave, down to the bottom of every column, and it spun the lights around. *Clank, clank, clank, clank,* hundreds of them, all turning on their metal stands, all at the same time, until every single one was pointing at the same place.
At the giant's face.
Three hundred lights blazed straight into that one huge eye.
Tepegöz screamed.
He threw his arms over his face and stumbled backwards. His heel caught on a fallen column. For a moment, he swayed there, enormous, waving his arms, like a tree in a storm.
Then he fell.

He crashed into the dark water with a splash so big that it soaked all three of us, even me, still on the walkway. A huge wave rolled across the whole cistern and slapped against the far walls. When it settled, he was gone, sunk down into whatever deep tunnel or hidden cave he had come from. All that was left was a big ring of bubbles, slowly spreading out across the water.
And then even the bubbles were gone.
We stood there, dripping and shaking, in the silence.
Drip. Drip. Drip.
The lights slowly turned back to their places, one by one, as if they were embarrassed.

Bora climbed out of the water onto the walkway, with a lot of grunting and puffing. He sat down, his clothes pouring water. He took the goldfish out of his shirt pocket and gently put it back in the water. It swam away, looking offended.
"Kuzey," said Bora finally, wringing out his shirt. "I'm really glad you're my friend."
"Me too," I said. And then, because my legs suddenly didn't work anymore, I sat down next to him.

Ela came and sat on my other side. Her braids were dripping and her glasses were crooked. Her hands were shaking. But she still had the parchment, held tight against her chest, and the Clue Book was still dry, because she had put it inside her shirt.
"Galata Tower," she said. Her voice wobbled, but only a little. "We need to get there before sunset tomorrow."

chapters.t: Chapter Eleven: Out of the Cistern
p: There is one problem with defeating a giant in a famous underground tourist attraction.
People notice.

By the time we had climbed the long stone staircase back up to the entrance, the sleeping ticket man was not sleeping anymore. He was standing in the doorway with his mouth open and his phone in his hand. Behind him, through the glass doors, I could see blue lights flashing in the rain.
"Police," whispered Ela. "Of course. He heard the noise."
"What noise?" said Bora. "You mean the giant screaming? Or the columns breaking? Or the three hundred lights going *clank clank clank?*"
"All of it, Bora."
The ticket man stared at us. Three kids, soaking wet from head to toe, one of them with water weed in his hair and a frosty sleeve.
"What," he said slowly, "happened down there?"
I opened my mouth. Nothing came out. How do you explain a one-eyed giant from a thousand-year-old story to a man who sells tickets?
Ela stepped forward and pushed her glasses up her nose.
"Earthquake," she said firmly.
The man blinked. "Earthquake?"

"A small one. Very local. Only under the cistern. We felt it. Some of the columns cracked, and we fell in the water. It was terrifying." She shivered dramatically. "You should probably check the columns. For safety. We'll just go home now. Our parents will be worried."
The ticket man looked at her for a long moment. Then he looked down the staircase into the dark, where something was still dripping and splashing, and he went pale.
"Earthquake," he agreed weakly. "Yes. That makes sense. More sense than... yes."
He stepped aside.
We walked very calmly past him, through the doors, past two police officers who were running in with flashlights, and into the rainy street. Then we turned the corner and ran as fast as we could.
"Ela," said Bora, panting. "You're scary sometimes."
"Thank you," said Ela.

We stopped under the dripping trees of a little park, behind the great dome of Hagia Sophia. The rain had stopped, but the wind was still blowing hard, scattering wet leaves everywhere. Down the hill, I could see the lights of the ferries crossing the dark water.
"Where do we go?" I said. "We can't go back to Grandma's. They'll be waiting there."
"And I can't go home," said Ela. "My dad's in Ankara at a conference until tomorrow night. The house is empty. If they know who I am, they'll know where I live."
We both looked at Bora.
Bora sighed. "My grandmother is home," he said. "She'll feed us. A lot. You've been warned."
On the ferry back across the Bosphorus, I stood at the railing in the dark and looked up.
On the roof of a building near the ferry station, something moved. A small figure, standing at the edge, against the orange glow of the city.
Pale hair, blowing in the wind.
It was Vera. She was watching our ferry. She didn't wave. She didn't call anyone on her phone, or point us out to a Gray. She just stood there and watched, as the ferry pulled away into the dark.
Then she turned and disappeared.
I didn't tell the others. I didn't know what it meant. But I thought about it all the way home.

chapters.t: Chapter Twelve: A Very Long Night
p: We spent the night at Bora's house.

His parents were away at a cousin's wedding in İzmir for the whole weekend, and the only person home was his grandmother, Fatma Nine. Fatma Nine is ninety-one years old and almost completely deaf. She thinks we're all "very nice boys," including Ela. She gave us dry clothes from a cupboard full of things that belonged to Bora's uncles in the 1980s, so I spent the night in a purple tracksuit with gold stripes, and Ela wore a sweater with a knitted picture of a horse on it.

Then Fatma Nine made us soup, and then more soup, and then pilaf, and then a cake, and then she fell asleep in her chair in front of a TV show about a family that argues a lot, and snored like a motorbike.
Bora was in heaven.
I couldn't eat anything.

Later, when the house was dark, I lay on the floor of Bora's room in a sleeping bag that smelled like mothballs. Bora was snoring in his bed, almost as loud as his grandmother. Ela was sitting by the window with a flashlight, reading the Clue Book.
I stared at the ceiling.
Every time I closed my eyes, I saw the frosted kitchen. Grandma's empty necklace chain, swinging in Mordecai's gray hand.
*Run, little Windborn! Run and find the Keys for me!*

I didn't realize I was crying until Ela sat down next to me. She didn't say anything. She just handed me a tissue from her pocket. Ela always has tissues. She also always has a pencil, a sharpener, a small screwdriver, three paperclips, a magnifying glass and an emergency chocolate bar. She says a detective has to be ready for anything.

"She'll be okay," Ela said quietly. "Grandma Nermin is the toughest person I know. Remember when the taxi driver tried to charge her double, and she made him drive her home for free *and* apologize to her cat?"
I laughed, even though I was still crying. It came out as a hiccup.
"Ela," I said. "What if I can't do this? What if I'm not a real Windborn? Tonight was luck. I don't even know how I did it."
Ela pushed her glasses up her nose and thought about this seriously, the way she thinks about everything.

"In the Tepegöz story," she said, "Basat wasn't the strongest warrior. Lots of stronger warriors fought the giant before him and lost. Basat won because he didn't try to fight like them. He looked for the weak spot." She shrugged. "Maybe you don't have to be the strongest. Maybe you just have to look for the weak spot."
"That was Bora's idea. The lights."
"Then we'll all look," she said. "That's what friends are for. Three people looking are better than one."
She went back to the window and the Clue Book.
I lay there for a while, listening to Bora snore. Then I got up quietly, went to the window, and opened it a crack.
The storm had passed. The night air was cold and clean and smelled of the sea. Far away, a ship's horn sounded on the Bosphorus.
"Wind," I whispered. "Are you there?"
For a long moment, nothing.
Then a soft breeze came in and moved the curtain.
*Always, Windborn.*
"Is my grandmother okay?"

The breeze went still, as if it was listening to something very far away. *She is alive,* it said finally. *She is cold, and far, in a gray tower by the sea. But she is not afraid. She is singing. I can hear her singing.*
I closed my eyes. I could almost hear it too. That crackly old Black Sea song.
"Thank you," I whispered.
*Sleep now, little one. Tomorrow you climb.*

I woke up at six to find Ela sitting on the floor surrounded by papers. The Clue Book was open. A map of Istanbul was spread out across the carpet. There were three empty tea glasses next to her, and a pencil stuck behind each ear.

"Okay," she said, before I even said good morning. "Galata Tower. Built in 1348 by the Genoese, who were traders from Italy. Sixty-seven meters tall. For hundreds of years, guards lived at the top and watched the city for fires, because Istanbul was made of wood and burned a lot. If they saw smoke, they'd hang a flag or beat a drum to warn everybody. That's the 'Galata's guards once watched for fire' part."
"Did you sleep at all?" I asked, yawning.

"Sleep is for people who aren't solving mysteries." She tapped the parchment. "'Look where the sun dies at the hour of the evening prayer.' The sun dies in the west. It sets. The evening prayer is the call to prayer at sunset. So we go to the top of the tower at sunset, during the evening call to prayer, and look west." She frowned. "But the tower is round. It has a balcony that goes all the way around. There must be something on the west side. Something you can only see at that exact time."
Bora came in carrying a tray. On it were eggs, cheese, olives, tomatoes, cucumbers, honey, jam, butter, and five simits.
"I made breakfast," he said proudly. "Fighting giants makes me hungry."
"Everything makes you hungry," said Ela, but she ate two simits.
We had all day before sunset. Ela wanted to spend it at the library. Bora wanted to spend it eating. But I had a different idea.
"I need to practice," I said.

So after breakfast, we climbed up to the flat roof of Bora's building. It was a sunny, windy morning, the kind of day when the whole city sparkles after a storm. Laundry flapped on lines on every roof around us. Far below, the streets were full of cars honking and simit sellers calling.
And on the edge of the roof sat about forty pigeons, all looking at us.
"Okay," I said. I held out my hand. "Wind. Can you... um... do something?"
Nothing happened. A pigeon pooped.
"Maybe ask it nicely," said Bora.
"I did ask it nicely."
"Maybe ask it *more* nicely."
I closed my eyes. I tried to remember what it felt like in the cistern. The fear. The wanting. But it's hard to feel desperate on a sunny rooftop after a big breakfast.
I tried for an hour.

By the end of the hour, I had managed to make one sock fly off a washing line. It landed on Bora's head. He said that it counted. Ela said it was probably just the normal wind. I agreed with Ela, and I was so frustrated that I kicked the roof door, which hurt my foot.
"It's not working," I said, hopping. "In the cistern, I didn't even try. It just happened."
Ela was watching me with her detective face. "What did you do in the cistern? Exactly?"
"I was scared. I wanted it so much. I wanted to save Bora."

"No," said Ela. "Before that. With the lights. You told us you *asked* it. You said 'help me, please.' And it said yes." She tapped her pencil against her chin. "Today you're trying to *make* it do things. Like a dog. Sit, stay, fetch. Maybe the wind doesn't like being told what to do. Does anyone?"
I thought about that. I thought about what Grandma had said. *The winds will learn to trust you.*

I closed my eyes again. This time, I didn't push. I just listened. I listened to the wind moving over the rooftops, through the laundry, around the chimneys. It was a happy morning wind, playful, a bit silly, full of the smell of the sea and fresh bread.
"Hello," I said to it. Just that. "I'm Kuzey. It's nice to meet you properly."
The wind stopped.

Then, all around us, the laundry on every washing line on every roof began to dance. Shirts waved their arms. Socks spun in circles. A pair of enormous underpants belonging to Bora's upstairs neighbor flapped like a flag. And all forty pigeons took off at once, swirling up into the sky in a great gray spiral, round and round over our heads, like a tornado made of birds.
*Hello, Windborn!* said the wind, and it was laughing. *We thought you would never say hello!*
Ela's mouth was open. Bora was clapping.
I was laughing too. For the first time since the storm, I was laughing.

chapters.t: Chapter Fourteen: The Old Man in the Bazaar
p: We had to get to Galata Tower by sunset. But first, Ela said, we needed information.

"We don't know anything about Mordecai," she said, as we walked down the hill toward the tram. "We don't know who the gray men are, what the Ashen Circle wants, or how many of them there are. A good detective never goes into a case without information."
"Where do we get information about secret evil wizards?" said Bora. "The internet?"
"I already tried the internet," said Ela, a little embarrassed. "There's a Mordecai Vane who sells used cars in Australia. I don't think it's him."

I had been thinking about this all morning. "Grandma used to go to the Grand Bazaar every Thursday," I said. "She always came back with nothing. No shopping bags. I asked her once what she bought, and she said, 'Conversation.' I thought she was being weird. But maybe..."
"Maybe she was meeting someone," said Ela. Her eyes lit up. "Someone from the Order."
So we went to the Grand Bazaar.

The Grand Bazaar, Kapalıçarşı, is one of the oldest and biggest covered markets in the world. It's like a city under a roof. Long, curving streets with painted ceilings, lit by lamps, packed with shops selling everything: carpets, gold, lamps made of colored glass, leather jackets, spices piled in pyramids, soaps shaped like fruit, chess sets, slippers with curly toes. Shopkeepers stand in their doorways calling to everyone who walks past. "Hello, my friend! Where are you from? Just looking is free!"
It was crowded and noisy and smelled of leather and cinnamon and apple tea.
"How do we find one person in here?" said Bora. "There are four thousand shops."
"We don't," I said. "The wind does."

There isn't much wind in the Grand Bazaar. It's covered. But there's a little. It slips in through the gates and the windows in the roof, and it wanders through the streets, very slowly, picking up all the smells. I closed my eyes and listened for it.
*The compass man,* it whispered. *The compass man in the street of the old clocks. Nermin's friend.*

We followed the little wind through the bazaar. Left, right, left, down a narrow street full of shops selling old clocks that all ticked at different times, under an arch, up three steps. It led us to a tiny shop at the end of a dead-end alley, so small that it was really more of a cupboard.
The window was full of compasses.

Old brass ships' compasses. Little pocket compasses. Compasses with mother-of-pearl faces and compasses with sundials. And in the middle of them all, carved into the wooden frame of the window, was a small compass rose with seven points.
"Seven points," whispered Ela. "Like the one on Grandma's needle."

Inside, an old man sat behind a counter, polishing a compass with a cloth. He was very thin and very old, with a white beard and a red fez, and little round glasses just like Ela's. He didn't look up when we came in.
"We're closed," he said.
"The sign says open," said Ela.
"The sign is a liar. It has always been a liar. I bought it from a liar." He held up the compass he was polishing and looked at it through his glasses. "Go away, children. This is not a toy shop."
I stepped forward. I didn't know what to say. So I just held out my hand, palm up, with the Yıldız Key on it.
The old man looked at it.
He put down the compass. He put down the cloth. He took off his glasses, cleaned them, and put them back on. He looked at the Key again. Then he looked at me, and his old eyes filled up with tears.

"Nermin's boy," he whispered. "The Windborn. So it is true. She told me, but I didn't believe her." He stood up, very slowly, and bowed to me. A real bow, from the waist, like I was a king. "My name is Rıza Usta. I have been a member of the Order of the Compass Rose for seventy years. Come in, children. Come in quickly. And close the door."

Rıza Usta's shop was bigger on the inside than it looked from the outside. Behind the counter, there was a door hidden behind a curtain, and behind the door was a little room with a carpet, cushions, a brass lamp and a tiny stove where he made us apple tea.

He listened to our whole story without interrupting once. When I told him about Grandma, he closed his eyes and said a quiet prayer. When Bora told him about Tepegöz, he laughed and slapped his knee. "The old one-eye is awake! Good! He has been lazy too long."
Then he told us what he knew.
"Mordecai Vane," he said, stirring his tea, "was once one of us."
We all stared at him.

"Forty years ago, he was a young man. Very clever. Very serious. He came to Istanbul to study, and your grandmother was his teacher. He loved the stories of the winds more than anyone I ever met. He read every book. He learned every language. He knew more about the Seven Keys than people who had been in the Order for fifty years." Rıza Usta shook his head. "But he wanted one thing more than anything in the world. He wanted to be a Windborn. And he was not born one."
"So what happened?" asked Ela, writing furiously.

"He became bitter. Angry. He said it wasn't fair that the winds chose some people and not others. One day he disappeared, and he took a very old, very dangerous book with him. A book that the Order had kept locked away for centuries. When he came back, years later, he had that gray hand. And he had started the Ashen Circle."
"What's the gray hand?" I asked. "What does it do?"

"It steals," said Rıza Usta simply. "A Windborn asks the wind, and the wind answers because it chooses to. The gray hand does not ask. It grabs a wind and squeezes it and freezes it until the wind has no choice but to obey. It's like..." He searched for the words. "It's like the difference between a friend who helps you, and a prisoner who is forced to work."
I thought of the frost on the chestnut cart. The frozen door shattering into a thousand pieces.
"And the gray men?" said Bora. "The ones with the foggy eyes?"

"We call them the Grays. They are ordinary people, once. Mordecai touches them with his hand, and the cold gets inside them. Into their heads. They forget who they are. They only remember to obey him." He shivered. "Be careful of them. They are not clever, but they never stop, and they never get tired."
"And the twins?" said Ela. "Vex and Vera?"

Rıza Usta's face grew sad. "His children. Their mother died when they were small. A good woman, I'm told. Since then, he has raised them alone, to be like him. The boy has his own gray glove now, a small one. The girl..." He shrugged. "I don't know about the girl. I have heard she asks a lot of questions. That is not a thing Mordecai likes."
I remembered Vera on the dock. The sad, curious way she had looked at me.

Rıza Usta put down his tea glass. He reached under a cushion and pulled out something wrapped in an old silk scarf. He unwrapped it carefully. Inside was a small brass compass, very old, with a cracked glass face and seven points instead of four.

"This was your great-great-grandfather's," he said, giving it to me. "Kaptan Murat. Your grandmother gave it to me to keep, years ago, in case something happened to her. It does not point north. It points to the nearest Key. Or to the nearest danger. Sometimes, it's hard to tell which."
I held it. The needle swung around slowly, and pointed at my pocket, where the Yıldız Key was.
Then it swung around again, very fast, and pointed at the door.
Rıza Usta's face went white.
"They're here," he whispered. "The Grays. They followed you."
Through the curtain, we heard the shop door open. The little bell above it tinkled. Then heavy footsteps. Many of them, all in step.
The temperature in the room dropped. Rıza Usta's apple tea grew a skin of ice.

"Through the back," whispered Rıza Usta. He pulled aside a carpet on the wall. Behind it was a tiny wooden door, barely big enough for Bora. "This goes to the old storerooms. Then out to the street of the carpet sellers. Go. Run. Don't stop until you are out of the bazaar."
"What about you?" said Ela.
The old man smiled. He picked up a heavy brass compass from the shelf, as big as a dinner plate, and weighed it in his hand.
"I am ninety years old, my dear," he said. "I have fought worse than a few gray men in suits. Your grandmother taught me a very good trick with compasses."

We went through the little door. Bora had to go sideways and suck in his stomach. Behind us, through the wall, we heard a voice say, "Where is the boy?" in a flat, cold voice, and then a lot of loud *bonk* sounds, and someone yelling.
The storerooms were dark and dusty and full of rolled-up carpets stacked to the ceiling. We ran through them, sneezing, and out through another door into a narrow street full of carpet shops.
And right at the end of the street, in their gray suits and gray hats, stood three Grays.
They turned toward us all at once, like puppets on strings. Their foggy eyes stared.
"Other way!" I shouted.
We ran the other way. Two more Grays came around the corner in front of us.
We were trapped.

The Grays walked toward us from both sides. Slowly. They weren't in a hurry. They didn't need to be. Frost spread out across the stone floor around their feet. The shopkeepers had all gone quiet and were pulling down their metal shutters, *clang, clang, clang.*
I took out Kaptan Murat's compass. The needle was spinning wildly.
"Kuzey," said Ela, very quietly. "Now would be a good time for wind."
"There's no wind in here! It's covered!"
But then I looked up.
Above us, the painted ceiling of the bazaar was curved, like a long tunnel. And all along the top, every few meters, there were little round windows. Some of them were open, to let in light and air.
I didn't push this time. I didn't grab. I just looked up at the little windows, and I said, as politely as I could, "Wind? Could you come inside for a minute, please? We're in a bit of trouble."
*A bit of trouble, he says!* said the wind outside, and it sounded delighted.
It came pouring in through every window at once.

It came down into the street like a waterfall, and it brought the whole bazaar to life. Every hanging carpet in every shop lifted off its hook. Hundreds of them. Red and blue and gold, big and small, flying through the air like a flock of enormous colorful birds. Silk scarves streamed past like ribbons. Glass lamps spun and jingled. A cloud of paprika and cumin exploded off a spice stall in an orange-red cloud.

The carpets swooped down on the Grays. They wrapped around them, one after another, rolling them up like börek, until there were five gray men lying on the floor, wrapped from neck to toe in very expensive carpets, sneezing from the paprika.
The shopkeepers came out from behind their shutters and stared.
"Sorry!" I called, as we ran past. "Sorry about the carpets!"
"Hey!" shouted one of the carpet sellers. "Those are handmade! From Kayseri!"
"They're very nice!" called Bora. "Very strong!"
We ran out of the bazaar through the Nuruosmaniye Gate, into the sunlight, and didn't stop running until we were three streets away.
Then we collapsed against a wall, gasping and laughing.
"*Carpets,*" said Ela. "You flew *carpets.* In the *Grand Bazaar.* Like a fairy tale."
"I just asked nicely," I said.
Bora was looking at the sky. The sun was already past the middle, starting its slow slide toward the west.
"Guys," he said. "Galata Tower. Sunset. We need to move."
We ended up at Eminönü, by the water, because Bora said he could not climb a single tower on an empty stomach, and because Ela said she needed "thinking food."

Eminönü is one of the busiest places in Istanbul. Ferries come and go every few minutes, blowing their horns. Thousands of people hurry past in every direction. Pigeons fight over crumbs outside the New Mosque. And right on the water, rocking up and down in the waves, are the fish sandwich boats.

They are old wooden boats, painted red and gold like little palaces, with huge grills on board. Men in old-fashioned costumes cook fish over the fire, and the smoke blows across the water, and the smell is so good that people come from the other side of the world just to stand there and sniff. They put the fish in half a loaf of bread with onions and lettuce, and hand it up to you over the side of the boat, and you eat it sitting on a tiny plastic stool by the water.
Bora ate two. Ela ate one. I held mine and didn't eat it.
"Kuzey," said Bora, with his mouth full. "Eat. Wind powers need fuel."
"I keep thinking about Rıza Usta," I said. "We just left him there. With the Grays. He's ninety years old."
Ela put down her sandwich. "He told us to go," she said. "Like your grandmother. Grown-ups in the Order keep telling us to run while they stay behind." She frowned. "I don't like it either."
We sat there for a while, watching the ferries. A seagull landed next to Bora and stared at his sandwich. Bora stared back. Neither of them blinked.
Then the wind changed.
It came off the water, from the Golden Horn, cool and salty. But inside it was something else. A faint smell of brass polish and apple tea.

*The compass man says hello,* whispered the wind. *He says the gray men left with very sore heads. He says there are compasses all over his floor now, and it will take him a week to sort them. He says he has not had so much fun since 1974.*
I laughed out loud. Ela and Bora looked at me.
"He's okay," I said. "Rıza Usta. He's okay. He beat them. With compasses."
"Like Grandma," said Ela, and she smiled. "It must be an Order thing."
"Can the wind always do that?" asked Bora. "Bring messages? Like a phone?"
"I don't know," I said. "I think so. Maybe. I think it's like the wind is everywhere, so it hears everything, and it remembers..."
I stopped.

Because a second breeze had come. A different one. It wasn't from the Golden Horn. It came from much, much farther away, from the north, across the sea. It was very thin and very tired, as if it had traveled for a very long time. It was cold and it smelled of fog.
And it carried a voice. A crackly old voice, very faint, like a radio station that is almost out of range.
*Tell him I'm all right. Tell him to wear a scarf.*
I sat completely still. The sandwich fell out of my hand. The seagull grabbed it and flew away in triumph.
"Kuzey?" said Ela. "What is it? What's wrong?"
I couldn't speak for a moment. Then I said, "It's Grandma. She sent a message. On the wind." My voice cracked. "She says she's all right."
Bora put his arm around my shoulders, a huge warm arm, and squeezed. Ela grabbed my hand.
"What else?" asked Ela. "Did she say where she is? Any clue? Anything?"
"She said," I swallowed. "She said to wear a scarf."
There was a pause.

Then Bora started to laugh, and Ela started to laugh, and I started to laugh too, so hard that tears came out, sitting on a tiny plastic stool by the water at Eminönü while the ferries hooted and the seagulls screamed and the fish smoke drifted over us.
"That," said Ela, wiping her eyes, "is the most grandmother message in the history of the world."

On the way to the tram, we passed a man selling scarves from a little cart. Bora bought me one with his last coins. It was bright orange with a picture of a football on it, and it was the ugliest scarf I have ever seen.
I wore it all day.

We took the tram across the Galata Bridge to Karaköy, then climbed the steep, crooked streets of Galata on foot. The streets there are so steep that some of them are stairs, and Bora had to stop three times to "look at the view," which meant breathe.

Galata Tower rises above the old roofs like a giant stone pencil with a pointy cone hat. It's been there for almost seven hundred years. It has seen earthquakes and fires and wars, and once, four hundred years ago, a man named Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi is supposed to have jumped off the top of it with wings he made himself and flown all the way across the Bosphorus to Asia.
"Do you think that's true?" said Bora, looking up at the top.
*It is true,* whispered the wind. *I carried him. He was very brave and very heavy. Like your friend.*
I didn't tell Bora that part.
There was a long line of tourists at the bottom of the tower, curling around the little square. My heart sank. "We'll never get in before sunset."
"Leave it to me," said Bora. He walked straight to the front of the line, to the ticket desk, where a young man in a uniform was selling tickets. "Mehmet Abi!"
"Bora!" The young man broke into a huge smile. "How's your mother? How's your grandmother? Still deaf?"
"Still deaf. These are my friends. Can we go up?"
Mehmet looked at the long line. He looked at us. He winked. "Staff entrance. Go on."
"Your cousin?" Ela asked, as we hurried through a side door.
"Second cousin," said Bora. "I have a cousin everywhere. Ankara, İzmir, Trabzon. Germany. Australia. My mom says if you dropped me anywhere in the world, I'd find a cousin in fifteen minutes."
It's like a superpower.

We rode the elevator up through the middle of the tower, squashed between a group of German tourists and a very tall man with a very large camera. Then we climbed the last narrow, winding staircase, round and round, and stepped out onto the balcony.
The whole city spread out below us.

I have lived in Istanbul all my life, but I had never seen it like that. The Golden Horn, the long harbor that cuts into the European side, glittered like a strip of gold foil. Across it was the old city on its seven hills, crowded with hundreds of domes and minarets, the great mosques sitting on the hilltops like giant gray hens with their chicks around them. To the east was the Bosphorus, and the ferries crossing it, and the green hills of Asia beyond. And far to the west, past the old city walls, the sun was sinking toward the Sea of Marmara in an orange blaze, turning the whole sky pink and gold.
"Wow," said Bora.
Even Ela put down her pencil.

The balcony was narrow, and it went all the way around the tower, with a stone railing about as high as my chest. Tourists were taking selfies everywhere. We pushed our way around to the west side and waited.
The sun sank lower. It touched the sea.
And then, from every minaret in the city at once, the evening call to prayer began.

It started with one voice, far away, rising and falling. Then another joined it, and another, and another, from every direction, hundreds of voices from hundreds of minarets, all singing at slightly different times, so the sound rolled over the rooftops like a wave, echoing off the water, filling the whole sky.
It was the most beautiful sound in the world. I had heard it every day of my life, and I had never really listened to it before.
"Now," Ela whispered. "Look west! Look for anything!"
We pressed against the railing on the west side. I looked at the old city. The water. The setting sun. Nothing. Just the view. A beautiful, ordinary view.
"I don't see anything," said Bora.
"Keep looking!"
And then the wind came. Warm and soft, this time, smelling of the sea.
*Not out, Windborn,* it whispered. *Down. The old guards left a mark. Look down.*
I looked down.

On the stone ledge just below the railing, on the outside of the tower, where nobody would ever look unless they were leaning over the edge, almost hidden under a pile of pigeon feathers and old leaves, there was something carved into the stone.
"Hold my legs," I said.
"What?" said Bora.
"Hold my legs. I need to lean over."
"We are SIXTY-SEVEN METERS UP!" said Bora, who had read that on a sign.
"Just hold them!"

Bora held my legs. Ela held Bora. I leaned over the stone railing, my stomach pressed against the cold stone, my head and arms hanging out over the city. Far, far below, people walked across the square like ants. A seagull flew past underneath me, which is a very strange thing to see.
I brushed away the feathers and leaves with my hand.

It was a tiny compass rose, carved into the stone, no bigger than my palm. Seven points, not four. It was very old, the edges worn soft by hundreds of years of rain. One point was much longer than the others. And in the light of the setting sun, at exactly that moment, the long point was glowing. Not with its own light. The sun was shining straight along it, through a little groove cut into the stone, so it lit up like a golden arrow.
It pointed straight at the setting sun.
§CLUE A seven-pointed compass rose, carved under the west railing of Galata Tower. At sunset, its long point glows like a golden arrow. Bearing: 285 degrees.
No. Not at the sun. At something under the sun. Something in the old city.
"Ela!" I called. "Your compass! Quick!"
She passed me her little compass, the one she always carries. I held it over the carving, lined it up with the long golden point, and read it out.
"Two hundred and... eighty? Two hundred and eighty-five degrees!"

"Pull him up!" said Ela, and Bora pulled me back over the railing so hard that we both fell on the floor of the balcony, and a German tourist stepped over us and said something that sounded like a complaint.

Ela was already on her knees with the map of Istanbul spread out on the stone floor. She put the compass on the map, right on Galata Tower, turned it to two hundred and eighty-five degrees, and drew a straight line with a ruler (of course she had a ruler) across the Golden Horn, through the old city.
The line ran straight through the middle of Sultanahmet. Past the Blue Mosque. Past Hagia Sophia.
Her pencil stopped.
"Kuzey," she said, and her eyes went wide. "It points to the Hippodrome. To the Serpent Column."

"The Serpent Column," I repeated. I knew it from school trips. A strange, twisted bronze pillar in the middle of the old Roman stadium. "Snakes," I said. "Medusa had snakes for hair. It's all snakes."
"Snakes have no heads," said Ela. She was frowning. "I mean, the Serpent Column. The heads were broken off hundreds of years ago. One of them is in the museum. Nobody knows where the others are."
"Very good," said a voice behind us. "You saved me a lot of thinking."
We spun around.
Vex Vane leaned against the doorway that led to the stairs, smiling his father's smile. Too many teeth. Behind him, arms crossed, stood his sister Vera.
And in Vex's hand was a gray glove, just like his father's. Only smaller.
"Give me the needles," said Vex, "and nobody gets thrown off a tower."

Up close, he looked even more like his father. Same sharp face. Same cold green eyes. Same smile that didn't reach his eyes. But he was only thirteen, and there was something about the way he stood, his shoulders very stiff, like he was trying very hard to look bigger than he was.
"We're not giving you anything," I said, stepping in front of Ela and the map.
"Oh, I think you are." Vex pulled on the gray glove. It was too big for him, I noticed. It wrinkled at the fingertips.

Cold fog began to pour from his fingers. It crawled across the balcony floor like smoke, white and freezing. The tourists around us shivered and pulled their jackets tight, looking up at the sky, not understanding. The German tourist said something about the weather.
Frost spread across the stone railing. My breath came out in clouds.

"My father says you're special," said Vex. "A Windborn. The first one in a hundred years." He laughed, but it wasn't a happy laugh. "You don't look very special to me. You look like a kid in a purple tracksuit."
I had forgotten I was still wearing Bora's uncle's purple tracksuit.
"Give me the needles," Vex said again, "or I'll freeze your friends. Starting with the fat one."
"Hey," said Bora. "I'm *big boned.*"
The fog crept toward Bora's feet. Frost climbed up his shoes. He tried to step back and couldn't. His feet were stuck to the floor.
"Stop it!" I said.

The wind inside me moved. I could feel it, cold and angry, the North Wind, the Yıldız, rising up in my chest like a wolf that's been woken up. My hands started to tingle. I could feel the power of it, the size of it, and for one terrible second I wanted to use it. I wanted to blow Vex right off the tower.
*No,* whispered the wind outside, very softly. *Not like him, little one. Never like him.*
But then Vera grabbed her brother's arm.
"Vex, not here," she said. "There are people everywhere. Father said no witnesses."
"Father isn't here."
"I am," said Vera firmly.
Vex turned to look at her, and for a second, the fog stopped. "Whose side are you on?"
"Yours," said Vera. "Always. That's why I'm telling you to stop."
They stared at each other. Brother and sister. Twins. I could see something going on between them, some kind of argument without words.
And while Vex was looking at his sister, Vera looked past him. Straight at me.
She gave the tiniest nod toward the stairs. So small that nobody else would have noticed. Like she was telling us to *go.*
I didn't wait to understand.
"RUN!"

I grabbed Bora's arm and pulled. The frost on his shoes cracked, and he stumbled free. Ela snatched up the map. We pushed through a group of Japanese tourists ("Sorry! Sumimasen!" Bora called, the only Japanese word he knew, which he had learned from a cartoon) and dived down the narrow staircase.
"VERA!" I heard Vex yell behind us. "You did that on purpose!"
We didn't wait to hear her answer.

We ran down the winding stairs, into the elevator, and jammed the button for the ground floor. The doors closed just as Vex came flying down the stairs after us, his gray glove raised, frost spraying from his fingers. It hit the closing doors and spread across them in a pattern of white feathers.
The elevator dropped.
"She helped us," said Ela, breathing hard. "Vera. She helped us. Why would she do that?"
"I don't know," I said.
But I kept thinking about her face. The sad, curious look. The tiny nod.
We burst out of the bottom of the tower and into the steep street. The sky was purple now. The streetlights were coming on.
"The Serpent Column!" Ela shouted. "Go!"
We ran.

Down the steep streets of Galata, past cafés and music shops, past a cat sleeping on a car roof and a man selling stuffed mussels from a cart. Bora was huffing and puffing like a steam train. Ela was holding her side. Behind us, we heard footsteps. Then a shout.
I looked back. Vex was at the top of the street. And behind him, coming around the corner, were more Grays. Four. Five. Six.
"They're following us!" I yelled.
"Of course they are!" Ela yelled back. "That's what *chasing* means!"
We ran all the way down the hill to the Galata Bridge.

The Galata Bridge crosses the Golden Horn, joining the new city to the old one. On the top level, there are cars and trams, and all along both sides stand fishermen, hundreds of them, in long rows, with their fishing rods hanging over the railings and their buckets full of little silver fish. They stand there all day and all night, in every kind of weather. Every kid in Istanbul has walked under those fishing lines.

We ran across the bridge between the fishermen. The water below was dark and glittering, reflecting the lights of the old city. Across it, the great mosques were lit up gold against the purple sky, like palaces in a dream.
Halfway across, I heard a crackling sound behind us.

I looked back. Vex was standing at the start of the bridge with his gray glove raised. Frost was spreading out from his feet, across the road, across the pavement, fast, like a white carpet unrolling. Cars skidded. A tram groaned to a stop. The fishermen shouted as their fishing lines froze stiff, and their buckets of water turned to ice with the fish still inside.
The frost was coming straight for us.
"Faster!" shouted Ela.
But Bora was slowing down. He was out of breath. He couldn't go any faster.
The frost reached his heels.
I stopped. I turned around. I stood between Bora and the ice.
And this time I didn't ask the wind for help. I asked it for something else.
"Wind," I said. "The fishermen. Please. Their lines."
*Clever boy,* said the wind.

It blew along the bridge, gently, all the way down the rows of fishermen. And it lifted every fishing line. Hundreds of them. Long, thin, invisible lines, with little hooks and weights on the ends. The wind swung them all through the air, crisscrossing, over and under, weaving them together like a giant spider's web across the whole bridge.
Vex ran straight into it.
And so did the Grays behind him.

They hit the web of fishing lines and bounced back, tangled up, arms and legs everywhere. The more they struggled, the more tangled they got. One Gray had three hooks stuck in his hat.
