Another one had a fish caught in his collar. Vex was wrapped up so tight that only his face was showing, red and furious, still shouting.
The frost stopped spreading. Without Vex's glove pointing at it, it started to melt.
The fishermen were staring at me.
"Sorry!" I called. "I'll... um... someone will untangle them!"
An old fisherman with a huge mustache took his cigarette out of his mouth. He looked at Vex, trapped in the net of lines. He looked at me. And he started to laugh.
"Thirty years I've been fishing on this bridge," he said, "and this is the biggest catch I've ever seen."
We ran the rest of the way across the bridge, into the old city, and didn't look back.

The Hippodrome was once a huge chariot-racing stadium, built by the Romans almost two thousand years ago. Back then, a hundred thousand people would sit there and scream for their favorite teams, the Blues and the Greens, while chariots pulled by four horses raced around the track. Sometimes the fans fought so much that they started riots and burned half the city down. (Bora said it sounded like football.)

Now the stadium is gone, and it's a long, wide park in Sultanahmet, with trees and benches and pigeons. But in the middle of it, where the center of the racetrack once was, three ancient monuments still stand in a row.
The first is the Obelisk of Theodosius, a tall pink stone needle from Egypt, three and a half thousand years old, covered with carvings of birds and eyes and snakes.
The third is the Walled Obelisk, a tall rough tower of stones.
And in the middle, between them, is the Serpent Column.

When we got there, it was dark. The park was almost empty. A few people were walking their dogs. A man was selling roasted corn from a cart, and Bora looked at it so sadly that I almost stopped to buy him some.

The Serpent Column stands in a little pit below the ground, surrounded by a low iron fence. It's a bronze pillar, about as tall as two men, made of three huge snakes twisted around each other like a rope. Their bodies coil around and around, all the way up. It is two thousand five hundred years old. It was made by the ancient Greeks, from the melted-down weapons of a defeated army, and it stood for centuries at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, until the Roman emperor Constantine brought it here.
Once, three snake heads rose from the top, spreading out in three directions.
But hundreds of years ago, the heads were broken off. Now the top of the column ends in a jagged, broken edge.
In the dark, under the streetlights, the bronze snakes glowed a deep, dull green.
I climbed over the little iron fence and dropped down into the pit. Ela and Bora kept watch at the top. Ela had the Clue Book out. Bora had his eyes on the corn.
It was quiet down there. Quiet and cool. The traffic noise of the city seemed very far away.
And the wind was waiting for me.
It was a different wind. Old, like the one in the cistern, but warmer. It smelled of sun and olives and the sea, a long way from here.
*I came with the snakes,* it whispered. *From Delphi. Long, long ago. I have been waiting for you, Windborn. The snakes have no heads. But they still have a heart.*
§CLUE The snakes have no heads, but they still have a heart.
"A heart," I said. "Where's the heart?"
*Feel for it.*

I put my hands on the cold bronze coils. I walked slowly around the column, feeling the twisting snakes under my fingers. They were smooth and cool, worn by centuries of rain and hands. I went around once. Nothing. I went around twice.
Halfway around the second time, my fingers found it.
A tiny hole, between two twisting snakes, right where their bodies crossed. Right at the height of my heart. You could only find it by touch. You would never see it in a hundred years of looking.
It was shaped like a jagged half-moon.
The shape of the broken needle from Medusa's box.
I took out the broken needle. My hands were shaking again. I looked up at Ela and Bora, peering over the fence above me.
"Do it," said Ela.
"Hurry," said Bora. "I can hear footsteps."
I pushed the broken needle into the heart of the snakes.

The ground rumbled. The bronze snakes seemed to *move,* slowly, uncoiling, their bodies sliding against each other with a long, low, grinding sound, like a huge clock being wound up. Dust trickled down from the edges of the pit.
And at my feet, a stone in the floor of the pit slid aside.
Below it was darkness. Stairs, carved into the rock, leading down.
And from the darkness came a sound like a thousand people breathing. In and out. In and out.
It was the wind. All the winds. Every wind I had ever heard, and hundreds I hadn't, whispering, sighing, singing, calling.
Calling my name.
*Kuzey. Kuzey. Kuzey.*
Ela and Bora climbed down into the pit, and we went down the stairs together, into the dark, holding hands. Even Ela. Even me.
There were exactly forty-nine steps. Ela counted. "Seven times seven," she whispered. "Of course."
At the bottom of the stairs was a small round room.

The walls were covered in a mosaic, made of thousands of tiny pieces of colored glass and stone. When Ela shone her flashlight on it, the whole room lit up, glittering blue and gold and green. The mosaic showed seven winds as faces, with puffed-out cheeks, blowing in seven directions. A cold silver face blowing from the north. A dark, stormy face blowing from the northwest. A warm golden face blowing from the southeast. And four more, each one different.

In the center of the room stood a stone pedestal. On it lay a map, painted on ancient leather, cracked and brown with age. It showed the whole world. Not the way maps look today, but the way they looked hundreds of years ago, with sea monsters in the oceans and strange shapes for the continents.
Seven places glowed faintly on it, like stars.
Istanbul. Athens. Iceland. Egypt. Japan. Mexico. And Cappadocia, in the very heart of Turkey, glowing brightest of all.
The star over Istanbul was already fading as we watched. Going dark. Like a candle being blown out.
"The hiding places," Ela breathed. "All seven. Kuzey, this is the map of the Keys. And the stars go out when a Key is found!"
Next to the map lay a letter. A modern one, in a white envelope, sealed with blue wax. On the front, in handwriting I knew better than my own: *For my Kuzey, when he is ready.*
My hands shook so much that I couldn't open it. Bora did it for me, very gently, and gave it back.
*My dear Kuzey,*

*If you are reading this, Mordecai has come, and I am probably his prisoner. Do not be afraid for me. I am tougher than I look, and I have been annoying that man for forty years. I can annoy him for forty more.*

*I came down here last spring, when the winds first started to whisper that you were ready, and I left this for you. I knew you would find it. You were always good at finding things. Remember the football?*

*You have the Yıldız Key, the North Wind. It is yours now, because a Windborn's Key becomes part of him. With it you will grow stronger. You will learn to speak to the winds, and they will learn to trust you. Never forget that trust is a gift. Mordecai has never understood that.*

*Six more Keys are hidden across the world. Mordecai has spies, money and terrible magic. But you have something he will never have: friends who would follow you into the dark. Keep them close. Listen to Ela. Feed Bora.*
*The next Key, the Lodos, the warm southwest wind, sleeps in the land where the winds were first given faces. Look for the tower where eight brothers blow.*
§CLUE The next Key, the Lodos, sleeps in the land where the winds were first given faces. Look for the tower where eight brothers blow.
*I love you to the North Star and back.*
*Grandma Nermin*
*P.S. Wear a scarf. It's November.*
I read it three times. The third time, I laughed at the P.S., and then I cried, and then I laughed again. Then I folded the letter carefully and put it in my pocket, next to my heart.
The Yıldız Key on my palm began to glow.

It started as a soft blue light, like moonlight on snow. Then it grew brighter, and brighter, until it lit up the whole room and made the mosaic winds sparkle. A cold, clean light ran up my arm, through my shoulder, into my chest. And for a moment I felt the whole wind of the north inside me. Enormous and wild and ancient, as big as the sky over the Black Sea, as cold as the stars.
And *friendly.* Like a giant dog that has decided you are its favorite person.
Then the light faded, and the Key was gone.
Not lost. *Inside* me.
When I breathed out, my breath came out frosty, in a little cloud that sparkled like snow.
"Whoa," said Bora.

"Eight brothers blowing," Ela was already muttering, writing in the Clue Book as fast as she could. "A tower of eight winds. The land where the winds were first given faces. Kuzey, I know this place. There's an ancient building in Athens, in Greece, called the Tower of the Winds. It has eight sides, and on each side there's a carving of a wind god. The Greeks gave every wind a name and a face. It's in my book about ancient wonders."
"Athens," I said. "Greece."

"We're eleven," said Bora. "And twelve. We can't just go to Greece. I don't even have a passport. Well, I do, but my mom keeps it in a drawer with the gold bracelets and the important papers, and I'm not allowed to touch that drawer."
From the stairs above came the sound of footsteps.
We froze. Ela switched off her flashlight. In the darkness, I felt Bora grab my arm. I took a breath and felt the North Wind stir inside me, ready.
And then a voice called down the stairs. Not the twins. Not a Gray. A man's voice, cheerful and slightly out of breath.
"Ela? Kuzey? Is that you down there? Your grandmother sent me a very strange text message yesterday. It just said 'Serpent Column, tomorrow night, bring snacks.' I thought it was a joke."
Ela's face lit up in the dark. "Dad!"

Uncle Tarık came down the stairs. He is Ela's father, my mother's brother, and an archaeologist at the university. He has wild hair that sticks out in every direction like he's been in a wind tunnel, a dusty jacket with patches on the elbows, glasses even thicker than Ela's, and a flashlight that he was holding upside down, so it was shining in his own face. He was carrying a big bag of snacks.
He looked at the mosaic. He looked at the map. He looked at the three of us. His mouth fell open.
"Is this," he said, in a whisper, "an undiscovered Byzantine wind chamber?"

"Yes," said Ela. "And Grandma's been kidnapped by an evil wizard with a stone hand, and Kuzey can control the wind, and we fought a giant in the Basilica Cistern, and we need to go to Athens. Tomorrow."
Uncle Tarık blinked several times. He looked at me. I breathed out, and a little cloud of frost sparkled in the air between us.
He blinked some more.
Then he sat down on the bottom step, opened the bag of snacks, and handed Bora a packet of crisps.

"Your grandmother," he said slowly, "always told me that our family had some very old, very strange secrets. I thought she meant recipes." He took off his glasses and cleaned them. He put them back on. Then he said, very seriously, "I have airline miles."

Uncle Tarık's apartment is in Moda, near the sea, and it is the messiest place I have ever been. There are books on every surface. Books on the chairs, books on the stairs, books in the bathtub. There are boxes of broken pottery he has dug up, labeled with things like *ROMAN JUG, PROBABLY* and *BYZANTINE?? ASK SELIN.* There's a plastic skeleton in the corner called Gerald, wearing a hat.
"Don't touch anything," said Ela, as we came in. "He knows where everything is. Supposedly."
"I absolutely do," said Uncle Tarık, and then he tripped over a box of Roman coins.

We had brought the leather map from the wind chamber. Uncle Tarık said it was the most important archaeological discovery of the century, and also that he would never be able to tell anyone about it, which made him look like he wanted to cry a little. He cleared the kitchen table by pushing everything onto the floor, and spread the map out under the lamp.
The seven stars glowed softly on the old leather. Six of them, anyway. The one over Istanbul had gone completely dark.
"One down," said Bora. "Six to go."
"Tell us about them, Dad," said Ela. "The places. All of them. You know everything about old places."

So Uncle Tarık told us. He pointed at each star in turn, and as he talked, his eyes got brighter and brighter, and his hands waved around, and he forgot all about being worried. This is what Uncle Tarık is like when he talks about history. It's like watching someone switch on a light.

"Athens," he said, pointing at the star in Greece. "The city of the ancient Greeks. Philosophers, theaters, temples on the hills. And the Tower of the Winds, the oldest weather station in the world. Two thousand years old. Eight sides, eight winds, each with a face and a name. The Greeks thought every wind was a god.

"Iceland," he went on, moving his finger far to the north, to an island near the top of the map. "Land of fire and ice. Volcanoes under glaciers. Geysers that shoot boiling water into the sky. The Vikings lived there, and they told stories of giants and trolls and gods who rode through storms.

"Egypt." His finger slid down to Africa, to the long green line of the Nile. "The Pyramids. The Sphinx. Five thousand years of kings and secrets and tombs nobody has found yet. The ancient Egyptians had a god of the air, called Shu, who held up the sky.

"Japan." All the way across to the right side of the map, to a long chain of islands. "Temples and mountains and shrines with thousands of red gates. The Japanese have a god of wind called Fūjin, who carries the winds in a bag on his back.

"Mexico." Across the whole ocean, to the other side of the world. "Pyramids again, but different ones. The Aztecs and the Maya and the people before them. They had a god called Quetzalcoatl. The Feathered Serpent. A god of the wind.

"And Cappadocia." His finger came back, all the way across the world, to Turkey, to the very middle of it. To the brightest star of all. "Fairy chimneys. Rocks shaped like towers, carved by the wind over millions of years. Churches inside the stone. And underground cities. Whole cities, under the ground, where thousands of people could hide."
He sat back.
"Wind gods," said Ela slowly. "Every single place on the map has a wind god. Or wind stories."

"Of course," said Uncle Tarık. "Every people in the world has told stories about the wind. Because you can't see it, and you can't catch it, and you can't control it." He looked at me, and then he quickly looked away again, as if he had said something rude.
"Some people can," said Bora.
"Six Keys," said Ela, writing a list in the Clue Book. "Six countries. Mordecai has money, spies, and a stone hand. We have Dad's airline miles."
"And Kuzey," said Bora.
"And Kuzey," Ela agreed. She looked at me over her glasses. "How many airline miles do you have, Dad?"
Uncle Tarık looked at the ceiling and did some sums in his head. "Enough," he said, "for most of the world. If we sit next to the toilets."
I looked at the map for a long time after the others went to bed. At the six glowing stars, scattered across the whole wide world.
The star over Cappadocia, in the middle of everything, was pulsing slowly. Brighter, then dimmer, then brighter again.
Like a heartbeat.

Uncle Tarık made us a very big dinner at his apartment that night, mostly from the snacks in the bag, plus some eggs, plus a jar of pickles, plus something from the freezer that he said was "probably lasagna." Bora ate three plates of it and said it was the best probably-lasagna he had ever had.
Then the problems began.

"Right," said Uncle Tarık, sitting down at the kitchen table with a notebook. He wrote *PROBLEMS* at the top of the page and underlined it twice. He and Ela are very alike. "Problem one. Bora's parents."

Bora's mother called at exactly that moment. From the wedding in İzmir. She was still in İzmir. She wanted to know if Bora was eating properly, if he was being polite to his grandmother, and if he had done his homework.
"Yes, yes and nearly," said Bora.

Then Uncle Tarık took the phone. He went into the next room and talked for ten minutes. I heard words like "educational," "archaeology" and "a wonderful chance to see the ancient world." When he came back, he was sweating, but he gave Bora a thumbs-up.
"School holiday next week anyway," he said. "She says you can come, if you call her every day, and if you wear a vest, and if I make sure you eat vegetables."
"I will eat so many vegetables," said Bora, who was eating a pickle.
"Problem two," said Uncle Tarık. He looked at me. "Your parents."
My stomach dropped.
It was Sunday night. And on Sunday nights, my parents called.

The video call connected at nine o'clock exactly. The screen showed a small metal room with a round window. Through the window, I could see white. Snow and ice, going on forever. My mom and dad were squashed together in front of the camera, wearing huge orange jackets, with their noses red from the cold.
"KUZEY!" they both shouted, at the same time.
Then the screen froze. My dad's face was stuck with his mouth open and one eye closed. It stayed like that for about ten seconds.
"...was a penguin THIS big," my mom's voice was saying, when it came back. "You should have seen it! It stole Dad's hat!"
"It was a very nice hat," said my dad sadly.

I laughed. I couldn't help it. For a minute, it was just a normal Sunday. They told me about the penguins and the ice and the scientist from Norway who snored. I told them about school. I didn't tell them about the storm, or the giant, or the carpets, or the man with the stone hand. I didn't know how.
"Where's Grandma?" asked my mom. "Is she there? Tell her I said hi."
My throat closed up. I couldn't speak.

Uncle Tarık leaned into the picture. "Hello, sister! Nermin's gone to visit some old friends for a few weeks," he said cheerfully. "So I'm taking the kids on a little trip during the school holiday. Greece. Very educational. Lots of ruins."
"Oh, how wonderful!" said my mom. "Kuzey, you'll love it! Make sure you wear sunscreen. And listen to your uncle. And..."
The screen froze again. This time on my mom, smiling, with her hand halfway through a wave.
I looked at her frozen face for a long time. My mom, at the bottom of the world, on the ice, smiling. Not knowing anything.
*It's all right, little one,* whispered the wind through the window. *You'll tell her one day. When she's home, and safe, and Grandma is with you.*
When the call came back, it was only for a second. "...love you, Kuzey! Love you to the..." Then it cut out completely.
To the North Star and back. That's what she was going to say. It's what Grandma always said. My mom got it from her.
I closed the laptop.
Ela put her hand on my shoulder. She didn't say anything. She didn't need to.

chapters.t: Chapter Twenty-Seven: Meanwhile, in the Gray Tower
p: *This is a part of the story that Kuzey didn't see. He only found out about it much later, from someone who was there.*
That same Sunday night, far to the north, the fog lay thick on the sea.

The tower stood on a lonely rock in a cold gray sea, far to the north. Nobody knew it was there. Ships sailed past it without seeing it, because a thick freezing fog wrapped around it all day and all night, every day of the year. Seagulls flew around it and did not land. Even the fish swam the long way around.
At the very top of the tower was a small round room with one window. There was a bed, a table, a chair and a small stove that gave almost no heat. The walls were covered in frost.
And in the chair, wrapped in three blankets, sat Grandma Nermin. Singing.

It was the old Black Sea song, the one about the fisherman who goes out on the sea and the girl who waits for him on the shore. She sang it softly, in her crackly voice, and as she sang, her breath made little clouds in the cold air.
The door opened. Mordecai Vane came in.

He had changed his long gray coat for a gray sweater, but he still wore the gray glove. He stood in the doorway for a long time, listening. Something moved on his face as she sang. Something that might, in another person, have been sadness.
Then it was gone.
"You always did like that song," he said.
"You always did sing it badly," said Grandma, without turning around.

Mordecai almost smiled. He came in and sat on the edge of the bed, across from her. Outside the window, the fog swirled. "Your grandson found the cistern," he said. "And the Galata Tower. And the Serpent Column. He's very good. Better than I expected. He even beat Tepegöz."
"Of course he did," said Grandma. "He's an Aydın. And he has friends."
"Friends." Mordecai said the word as if it tasted strange. "Friends won't help him when he stands in front of the Gate, Nermin. When he has to choose."
"Neither will a stone hand."
The cold in the room grew sharper. Frost crept across the table.
"You could make this so much easier," said Mordecai quietly. "Tell me where the other Keys are. All of them. You know. I know you know. And I will let you go home. I will leave the boy alone."
Grandma turned around in her chair, at last, and looked at him. Her brown eyes were sharp and steady.

"Mordecai," she said. "When you were nineteen years old, you came to my kitchen every Tuesday, and we drank tea, and you told me about every book you had read that week. You were the cleverest student I ever had. You were kind to Paşa's grandmother, who was a very bad-tempered cat. You helped old Rıza carry his boxes up the stairs. I was very fond of you." She paused. "I still am."
Mordecai went very still.
"That's why I will never tell you anything," said Grandma Nermin gently. "Because I want you to stop. And one day, I think you will."
For a long moment, nobody said anything. The fog pressed against the window.
Then Mordecai stood up, very fast, and walked to the door. "We'll talk again tomorrow," he said, without looking back.
"We'll talk every day," said Grandma. "I have nowhere else to be."
The door closed. The key turned in the lock.

Grandma Nermin sat in the cold for a while. Then she got up, went to the little window, and opened it a crack. The fog came in, wet and freezing. But underneath the fog, very faint, there was something else. A tiny breeze. A thin thread of wind from far away, from the south.
She leaned close to it and whispered.
"Tell him I'm proud of him. Tell him I'm still singing."
The breeze slipped out of the window, through the fog, over the gray sea, and began its long journey south.

Outside the door, on the cold stone stairs, a girl with pale hair sat alone. She had come back that evening through the fog, the way her father always traveled, cold and fast and silent. Now she sat with her knees pulled up to her chin. She had been there the whole time. Listening.
When her father came out, she pretended to be tying her shoe.
He walked past her without a word.
Vera Vane sat on the stairs for a long time after that, thinking about tea on Tuesdays, and a young man who had once been kind to a bad-tempered cat.
On Monday morning, before anything else, I made Uncle Tarık take me back to Grandma's apartment.
"Kuzey, it might not be safe," he said. "They might be watching it."
"I need my passport," I said. "And my clothes. And..." I stopped. "And I need to see it."
He looked at me for a moment. Then he nodded.

Ela and Bora came too. Of course they did. We went in through the back, through the courtyard with the cats, and up the old fire stairs. I went first this time. The kitchen window was still open. Rain had come in during the night, and the floor was wet.
I climbed inside.

The frost was gone. The broken door was lying in pieces in the hallway, melted into puddles. Everything else was exactly where it had been. The teacups on the table. Grandma's apron hanging on its hook. The newspaper, open to the crossword, with half the answers filled in her neat handwriting. Seven across: *A wind from the north (6).* She had written *POYRAZ* in pencil.
And the kettle. On the stove. Cold.
I had never seen that kettle cold in my whole life.

The nine compasses were scattered across the floor. One of them was broken, its glass cracked. I picked them up one by one and put them back on the shelf, in the right order, the way she liked them. Ela and Bora helped. Nobody talked.
When the last compass was on the shelf, something brushed against my legs.
Paşa the cat. He was sitting on the floor, looking up at me with his big yellow eyes. He meowed. A small, sad meow, not like his usual angry one.
"I know," I said. I picked him up. He let me, which he never does. "I miss her too."
Bora came over and scratched Paşa behind his ears. Then he frowned. "Kuzey. Who's going to feed him?"
I hadn't thought of that.
"The neighbor downstairs," said Ela. "Mrs. Aksoy. She loves cats. I'll ask her."
I put Paşa down. He went straight to the cold stove and sat in front of it, waiting, the way he always did, for the kettle to boil and Grandma to give him a bit of cheese.

I went to my room and packed. Passport, from the drawer. Clothes. My toothbrush. My football shirt. And from Grandma's room, after a long time of standing in the doorway, I took one more thing: her blue scarf with the little white flowers, the one she wore on cold days.
I wrapped it around my neck.

On my way out, I stopped by the wall of photographs in the hallway. There were hundreds of them, old and new, in frames of every size. Me as a baby. My parents' wedding. Grandma as a young woman, on a boat, laughing, with the wind in her hair. Grandma in front of the Pyramids. Grandma with a group of students in front of a university, a long time ago, everyone serious in black and white.
I didn't look closely at that one. I wish I had.
But I didn't know yet what I was looking for.
Before we left, I went back to the kitchen and stood in front of the stove.
I filled the kettle with water. I lit the gas. And I waited, until it started to hum, and then to whistle, and steam poured out of the spout and filled the kitchen with a soft warm cloud.
"What are you doing?" whispered Bora.
"Grandma says a kitchen without boiling tea is just a room with a fridge in it," I said.
I turned the gas down very low, so it would keep warm for a long time. Then I followed the others down the fire stairs.
Behind us, in the window, the kettle kept singing.
Istanbul Airport is so big that it has its own weather. At least, that's what Bora said, after we had walked for twenty minutes and still hadn't found our gate.

Uncle Tarık had used his airline miles to buy four tickets to Athens, on a flight at four o'clock on Monday afternoon. He kept checking the tickets every five minutes, as if they might disappear. He also kept checking his pockets for his passport, his phone and his glasses, which were on his head.
Ela was reading a guidebook about Athens. She had bought it at the airport bookshop with her own money. She had already put sticky notes on thirty-two pages.
Bora was eating. He had found a shop that sold baklava in little boxes, and he had bought four boxes. "For the journey," he said. "And emergencies."
I was watching the windows.

The wind outside the airport was strange and busy and confused. Airport winds are like that, Ela said later: all the planes going up and down churn them up, and they never get any peace. They were whispering a hundred different things at once, about clouds and runways and the weather in Paris. But under all of that, again and again, I heard one word.
*Gray. Gray. Gray.*
"Ela," I said quietly. "They're here."
She didn't look up from her guidebook. "Where?"
I looked around the huge, shining hall, at the thousands of people walking past with their suitcases. Families. Businesspeople. A football team in matching tracksuits. A group of nuns.
And there, standing completely still by a coffee shop, a man in a gray suit and a gray hat, holding a gray umbrella. Inside an airport. Where it never rains.
Then I saw another one, by the toilets. Another, near the escalator. Another, at the security gates, watching every face that went past.
"Four," I said. "No. Five."
Uncle Tarık went pale. "What do we do?"
Ela closed her guidebook. "They're looking for a boy and a girl and a big kid, with a man with wild hair," she said. "So we split up. And we change how we look."

Ten minutes later, Ela was wearing Uncle Tarık's jacket and a baseball cap with her braids tucked inside it. Bora was wearing a souvenir T-shirt that said I ♥ ISTANBUL and a pair of enormous sunglasses. Uncle Tarık had flattened his hair with water from a drinking fountain, which made him look like a completely different person, a person who had fallen in a lake. And I had Grandma's blue scarf wrapped all the way up over my nose, and a newspaper.
We went through security one at a time, a few minutes apart.
The Gray at the security gate looked straight at me. His foggy eyes moved slowly over my face. I felt frost prickle on the back of my neck.
*Breathe slowly, little one,* whispered the wind. *Look bored. Think about homework.*
I thought about homework. I thought about fractions. I thought about the long, boring list of the rivers of Turkey that Ms. Demir made us learn. Kızılırmak. Sakarya. Yeşilırmak. Fırat. Dicle.
The Gray looked away.
I walked through.

Twenty minutes later, the four of us were in our seats, squashed together at the very back of the plane, next to the toilets. Bora had the window. He had his eyes shut tight already, holding the armrests, even though we were still at the gate.
"Bora," said Ela. "We haven't even moved."
"I'm preparing," said Bora.
The plane rolled slowly out to the runway. The engines roared. And we began to move, faster and faster, the airport buildings rushing past outside the window, the whole plane shaking and rattling.
Then the wheels left the ground.

And at that exact moment, I felt it. A huge, warm gust of wind, rising up under the wings, lifting us. Not the normal wind. *My* wind. The North Wind, the Yıldız, and with it all the winds of Istanbul, the Poyraz from the Black Sea and the little cistern wind and the warm wind from Delphi, all of them together, pushing us up into the sky like a hand under a paper plane.
The plane leaped upward so smoothly that the passengers clapped. The captain came on the speaker sounding surprised. "Ah, ladies and gentlemen, we seem to have a very... helpful tailwind today."
Bora opened one eye. Then the other.

Below us, Istanbul spread out like a map. The Bosphorus, shining. The bridges, tiny as toys. The Golden Horn, the old city on its hills, the domes and minarets catching the afternoon sun. And somewhere down there, in Kadıköy, on the fifth floor, a kettle was still singing.
*Go well, Windborn,* said the winds of my city. *Come home safe. And bring her back to us.*
"I will," I whispered against the window.
Ela was already asleep on Uncle Tarık's shoulder, the Clue Book on her lap. Uncle Tarık was asleep too, with his mouth open. Bora was opening his first box of baklava.
I took out Grandma's letter, and read it one more time.
*Look for the tower where eight brothers blow.*
That's how it started.
The night a storm told me my name. The night my grandmother vanished. The night we fought a giant and flew carpets and caught a villain in a fishing net, and found the first of the Seven Winds.
Far below, the Aegean Sea glittered in the sun, and the plane flew south, toward Greece, toward the land where the winds were first given faces.
I pressed my forehead against the window, Grandma's scarf around my neck.
"I'll find her," I told the wind. "I promise."
*We know,* it said. *And when you find the Keys, little Windborn, you will have to choose what to do with them. Remember that. Choose well.*
Far away, in a cold gray tower by the sea, Mordecai Vane looked at a map just like ours. He watched the star over Istanbul go dark. And he smiled with too many teeth.
The race was on.
§END To be continued in Book Two: The Tower of the Winds.

For hundreds of years, sailors on the Black Sea, the Bosphorus and the Mediterranean used a wind rose to name the winds. Each wind had its own name and its own personality, and every sailor knew them by heart. These are the seven winds of the Order of the Compass Rose.
**Yıldız (North).** Named after the North Star, *yıldız* means "star." A cold, clear, starry wind. Kuzey's own wind.
**Poyraz (Northeast).** The great wind of the Black Sea. When the Poyraz blows hard, the fishermen go home and the ferries rock.
**Gündoğusu (East).** "Sunrise." The wind that comes from where the sun is born each morning.
**Keşişleme (Southeast).** Named after the monks, the *keşiş,* who lived on the mountains to the southeast. A warm, dry wind from the deserts.
**Kıble (South).** The wind from the direction of Mecca. Hot, and full of sand.
**Lodos (Southwest).** A warm, wild, wet wind that brings big waves and headaches. People in Istanbul say the Lodos makes everyone grumpy.
**Karayel (Northwest).** "Black wind." A stormy, dark wind that brings clouds and sudden rain.
And the eighth, the west wind, the **Batı**, the one that would not make a deal? Nobody knows. It is still wild. That is another story.

chapters.t: The Real Places in This Book
p: Almost everything in this book is real, except the giants, the magic and the wind talking. (Probably.)

**The Basilica Cistern.** A real underground water palace in Istanbul, built about 1,500 years ago, with 336 columns standing in water and fish swimming between them. At the back, two columns really do stand on giant stone heads of Medusa, one sideways and one upside down. Nobody knows for sure why they were put there.

**Galata Tower.** Built in 1348. For centuries, fire watchers lived at the top and looked out over the wooden city for smoke. There's a famous story that, about 400 years ago, a man named Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi strapped on wings he had made himself, jumped from the tower and glided all the way across the Bosphorus to Asia.
**The Grand Bazaar.** One of the oldest and biggest covered markets in the world, with about 4,000 shops and more than 60 streets under one roof. People really do get lost in it.
**Eminönü.** The fish sandwich boats really are there, rocking on the water by the Galata Bridge, and the fishermen really do line the bridge every day, in every weather.

**The Hippodrome and the Serpent Column.** The Hippodrome was a huge Roman chariot-racing stadium. Now it's a park in Sultanahmet, with three ancient monuments in the middle. The Serpent Column is made of three twisted bronze snakes, brought from Delphi in Greece. It's about 2,500 years old. The snakes' heads were broken off long ago; one of them is in the Istanbul Archaeology Museum.

**Tepegöz.** The one-eyed giant comes from *The Book of Dede Korkut,* a collection of old Turkish stories more than a thousand years old. In the story, the hero Basat defeats him by aiming for his only eye.
*Here is the first chapter of the next book,* The Tower of the Winds.
**Chapter One: Wind in My Pocket**
Here is something nobody tells you about having the North Wind living inside you: it makes airplane food cold.

Every time I breathed on my tray, the rice froze. The chicken grew little white crystals. The orange juice turned into an orange ice lolly. The flight attendant on the plane to Athens looked at my frozen rice, then at me, then at the frost growing on my window in the shape of tiny ferns, and decided not to ask.

"You have to learn control," said Ela from the seat next to me. She had the Clue Book open on her tray table, covered in notes about Greek wind gods. "Yesterday you sneezed and blew the curtains off Dad's window."
"That was an accident."
"So was the ferry seagull."
The ferry seagull was a sensitive subject. Let's just say I sneezed again, on the ferry to Moda, and a seagull flew backwards for about a hundred meters with a very surprised face.

Across the aisle, Bora was eating his own dinner, then mine (he said frozen rice was "like a crunchy snack"), then the one the old lady next to him didn't want. She was Greek, and she was so happy to see a boy who loved food that she gave him half a bag of pistachios and pinched his cheek. Bora told her she was very kind. She didn't speak Turkish, and Bora doesn't speak Greek, but somehow they understood each other perfectly. Bora is like that.
Uncle Tarık sat in the row in front of us, snoring with his mouth open, a book called *Ancient Greek Weather Towers* on his face.
It had been two days since Grandma Nermin disappeared. Only two days. It felt like two years.
I still had her letter in my pocket. I had read it so many times that the paper had gone soft as cloth.
I reached into my jacket for it, and my fingers touched something else. A small folded paper I had never seen before. It was tucked deep into the inside pocket, behind Grandma's letter.
I opened it. The handwriting was neat, sharp and unfamiliar. Little straight letters, all leaning slightly forward, like they were in a hurry.
*He keeps her in a gray tower by the sea. She is alive. She is not hurt. I'm sorry. Please don't tell anyone I wrote this. — V*
I read it three times. Then I showed it to Ela.
She read it twice, and her eyebrows climbed so high they nearly reached her braids.
"V," she said. "Vex or Vera."

"Vera," I said. I remembered her on Galata Tower, holding her brother's arm. Giving me that little nod toward the stairs. And on the roof, watching our ferry leave, not calling anyone. "It has to be Vera."
"When did she put it in your pocket?"
I thought about it. "On the tower. When we pushed past them to get to the stairs. She was right next to me."

"So she wrote it *before* she came to the tower," Ela said slowly. "She planned it." She tapped her pencil against her teeth, which is what she does when she's thinking very hard. "Kuzey. Either Vera Vane wants to help us, or this is a trap. A very clever trap. Maybe her father told her to write it, so we'd trust her. So we'd lead them to the Keys."
"She looked sad," I said. "On the dock. And on the tower."
"Villains can look sad," said Ela. "In books, the sad-looking ones are the most dangerous."
"This isn't a book."
"Everything is a book," said Ela, "if you write it down."

I looked out the window at the clouds. The wind out there was talking, a thousand voices in a language I almost understood. Up here, so high, the winds were fast and cold and very busy, rushing around the world like people late for a train.
"Maybe," I said, "it's both. A trap and help. Maybe she doesn't know which side she's on."
Ela looked at me for a long moment. Then she wrote something in the Clue Book. I leaned over to see.
*Vera Vane: ??? Keep watching.*
§END To be continued in* The Tower of the Winds...
